# How to use this guide

Applied Nutrition and Dietetics is a second-semester subject of the INC 2021 B.Sc Nursing curriculum (3 credits, 60 hours: 45 hours theory and 15 hours lab). It is examined in a **combined university paper with Applied Biochemistry**: Applied Biochemistry is **Section A (25 marks)** and Applied Nutrition and Dietetics is **Section B (50 marks)** of one 3-hour, 75-mark paper. Nutrition carries two-thirds of that paper, so give it about two-thirds of your preparation time for the combined exam.

**How the units are arranged.** The INC syllabus has thirteen units, several of them only 2–3 hours. They are joined into eight notes files:

| Notes file | INC unit(s) | Hours |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Unit 1 Introduction to nutrition, nutrients and foods | I | 2 |
| Unit 2 Carbohydrates, energy, proteins and fats | II + III + IV | 3 + 3 + 2 |
| Unit 3 Vitamins and minerals | V + VI | 3 + 3 |
| Unit 4 Balanced diet and nutrition across the life cycle | VII | 7 + 8 lab |
| Unit 5 Nutritional deficiency disorders | VIII | 6 |
| Unit 6 Therapeutic diets | IX | 4 + 7 lab |
| Unit 7 Cookery rules, preservation of nutrients and food safety | X + XIII | 3 + 2 |
| Unit 8 Nutritional assessment, nutrition education and national programmes | XI + XII | 4 + 3 |

Study one notes file a day: read it, write the "Remember" list from memory, then answer the questions and MCQs for that unit without looking.

**Section B: Applied Nutrition and Dietetics (50 marks)** — as given in INC Regulations 2020, Appendix 3. There is no internal choice, so every question must be answered. Your university may print it differently; confirm with your university.

| Part | What it asks | Marks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| MCQ | 8 multiple-choice questions | 8 × 1 = 8 |
| Essay | 1 long answer | 1 × 10 = 10 |
| Short | 4 short answers | 4 × 5 = 20 |
| Very short | 6 very short answers | 6 × 2 = 12 |
| **Total** | | **50** |

Section B takes about two-thirds of the 3-hour paper, so the mock test here is timed at 120 minutes. The university exam is 75 marks (Biochemistry 25 + Nutrition 50) with 25 internal marks. You must pass theory with at least 50%. The 15 lab hours (meal planning, balanced and therapeutic diets, low-cost dishes) are assessed internally; they are not a separate practical exam.

**About the numbers in these notes.** Energy, protein and micronutrient requirements are the **ICMR-NIN 2020** values (Nutrient Requirements for Indians — RDA and EAR). Many older textbooks still give the 2010 values (e.g. protein 1 g/kg, iron 17 and 21 mg); write the 2020 values but you may mention that they were revised. Where an official figure could not be confirmed, the notes describe the point without a number and tell you where to check. No drug doses are given; supplements in national programmes follow the current MoHFW/NHM schedule.

**Probability ratings**

- **High** — a favourite; comes up in most papers in some form. Learn the full answer with a table or flow diagram.
- **Medium** — appears every few papers or as part of a bigger question.
- **Low** — less common, but useful for MCQs and very short answers.

These ratings are estimates from syllabus weight and the usual style of nursing nutrition papers. They are not a promise of what will be asked.

**Where the marks usually come from**

| Notes file | Topics that keep coming back |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | Definitions (nutrition, nutrient, malnutrition, balanced diet), classification of nutrients and foods, factors affecting nutrition |
| 2 | Functions and sources of carbohydrates, proteins and fats; essential amino acids; BMR and its factors; calorie values; essential fatty acids |
| 3 | Vitamin A, D, C, B1 — functions, sources, deficiency; iron, calcium, iodine; fat- vs water-soluble vitamins |
| 4 | Balanced diet and its principles; RDA uses and limitations; diet in pregnancy and lactation; anaemia in pregnancy; IYCF and complementary feeding; food exchange; dietary fibre |
| 5 | PEM (kwashiorkor vs marasmus, SAM criteria, ten steps), vitamin A deficiency (xerophthalmia grades), anaemia, IDD, rickets |
| 6 | Therapeutic diet definition and types; diet in diabetes, hypertension/CVD, renal failure, liver disease, diarrhoea, post-operative; NG feeding |
| 7 | Methods of cooking; preventing nutrient loss; adulteration and tests; PFA/FSSA; five keys to safer food; food preservation |
| 8 | ABCD of nutritional assessment; anthropometry (MUAC, BMI); nutrition education; ICDS; AMB; NIDDCP; PM POSHAN; WIFS; role of the nurse |

**Scoring tips for this subject**

1. **Use tables** for comparisons — kwashiorkor vs marasmus, fat- vs water-soluble vitamins, cooking methods, ICDS services. A neat table earns marks quickly.
2. **For every nutrient answer use the same order**: definition → classification → functions → sources → requirement (ICMR-NIN 2020) → deficiency → excess. Examiners look for this structure.
3. **For every disease-diet answer use**: objectives → principles (what to give more, what to restrict) → foods allowed → foods to avoid → a short sample day menu → nurse's role.
4. **Give Indian, low-cost foods** — ragi, bajra, amla, guava, drumstick leaves, garden cress seeds, groundnut, sprouts, jaggery. Examiners like local examples.
5. **Learn the key numbers**: 4/4/9 kcal per gram; man 2110 and woman 1660 kcal (sedentary); protein 0.83 g/kg; pregnancy +350 kcal; lactation +600 kcal; SAM MUAC below 11.5 cm; anaemia in pregnancy Hb below 11 g/dL; Indian BMI obese at 25.
6. **Always end with the nurse's role** in deficiency and programme questions — assessment, delivery of services, education, referral, records.
7. **Very short answers (2 marks)**: one-line definition plus one example or fact.
8. **For programme questions** give: year started, ministry, beneficiaries, components/services, nurse's role. Learn ICDS's six services and AMB's 6 × 6 × 6.
9. MCQs come from small facts — read every "Remember" list the night before.

# Last-night revision sheet — Applied Nutrition and Dietetics

## 1. Basics
- **Nutrition**: science of food and its relation to health. **Nutrient**: chemical in food needed for energy, growth, repair, regulation.
- **Malnutrition** = under-nutrition, over-nutrition, imbalance, specific deficiency. India has a **double burden**.
- **Macronutrients**: carbohydrate, protein, fat. **Micronutrients**: vitamins, minerals. **Organic**: CHO, protein, fat, vitamins; **inorganic**: minerals, water.
- Foods by function: **energy-giving, body-building, protective**. Basic four groups: cereals; protein foods; vegetables and fruits; fats, oils, sugar.

## 2. Energy and macronutrients (ICMR-NIN 2020)
- kcal/g: carbohydrate **4**, protein **4**, fat **9**, alcohol **7**. 1 kcal = 4.184 kJ.
- Energy: man **2110/2710/3470**, woman **1660/2130/2720** (sedentary/moderate/heavy); pregnancy **+350**; lactation **+600** (0–6 m), **+520** (7–12 m).
- **BMR**: energy at complete rest; ↑ thyroxine, fever (~13% per °C), growth, pregnancy, cold, lean mass; ↓ starvation, age, hypothyroidism, sleep.
- Protein RDA **0.83 g/kg/day** (EAR 0.66): man **54 g**, woman **45.7 g**; pregnancy **+9.5 g** (2nd), **+22 g** (3rd trimester); lactation +16.9 g then +13.2 g.
- **Essential amino acids (8)**: isoleucine, leucine, lysine, methionine, phenylalanine, threonine, tryptophan, valine (+ histidine in infants). Cereals lack **lysine**, pulses lack **methionine** → combine. Cereal : legume : milk ≈ 3 : 1 : 2.5.
- Visible fat **20–50 g/day**; EFAs = **linoleic (n-6)** and **alpha-linolenic (n-3)**; trans fats most harmful.

## 3. Vitamins and minerals (RDA 2020, sedentary man / woman)
| Nutrient | RDA | Deficiency |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Vitamin A | 1000 / 840 µg | Night blindness, Bitot's spots, keratomalacia |
| Vitamin D | 600 IU | Rickets, osteomalacia |
| Vitamin K | — | Bleeding, newborn haemorrhage |
| Thiamine | 1.8 / 1.7 mg | Beriberi |
| Riboflavin | 2.5 / 2.4 mg | Angular stomatitis |
| Niacin | 18 / 14 mg | Pellagra (dermatitis, diarrhoea, dementia) |
| Folate | 300 / 220 µg | Megaloblastic anaemia, neural tube defects |
| B12 | 2.2 µg | Megaloblastic anaemia, neuropathy (only animal foods) |
| Vitamin C | 80 / 65 mg | Scurvy (amla richest) |
| Calcium | 1000 mg | Rickets, osteoporosis, tetany (milk, ragi) |
| Iron | 19 / 29 mg | Anaemia (vitamin C helps, tea hinders) |
| Iodine | 150 µg | Goitre, cretinism (iodised salt) |
| Zinc | 17 / 13 mg | Growth failure, poor healing |
- Salt below **5 g/day** (WHO). Fluoride: too little → caries; too much → fluorosis.

## 4. Balanced diet and life cycle
- **Balanced diet**: variety of foods meeting all needs + small safety margin. Principles: adequacy, balance, variety, moderation, calorie control, nutrient density, individualisation.
- **RDA** covers nearly all healthy people; limitations: healthy only, reference weights, not individual need. **EAR** for assessing groups.
- **Food exchange**: interchangeable portions (cereal 30 g ≈ 100 kcal, 3 g protein; pulse 30 g ≈ 100 kcal, 6 g protein).
- Nutritive value = **(nutrient per 100 g × amount) ÷ 100** (IFCT).
- **IYCF**: breastfeed **within 1 hour**, **exclusive 6 months**, complementary **from 6 months**, continue **2 years+**.
- **Anaemia in pregnancy**: Hb **< 11 g/dL** (severe < 7). Iron-rich foods + vitamin C, no tea with meals; IFA under AMB (counsel: after food, black stools harmless, keep away from children).
- Elderly: fewer calories, same protein, soft food, fluids, fibre.

## 5. Deficiency disorders
- WHO: **wasting** WFH < −2 SD (acute); **stunting** HFA < −2 SD (chronic); **underweight** WFA < −2 SD. NFHS-5: 35.5% / 19.3% / 32.1%.
- **SAM** (6–59 m): WFH < −3 SD **or** MUAC < **11.5 cm** **or** bilateral pitting oedema. MAM: MUAC 11.5–12.5 cm.
- **Kwashiorkor**: oedema, flaky paint skin, fatty liver, moon face, apathy. **Marasmus**: severe wasting, no oedema, old-man face, alert, hungry.
- **Ten steps**: hypoglycaemia, hypothermia, dehydration (ReSoMal), electrolytes, infection, micronutrients (iron later), cautious feeding (F-75), catch-up (F-100/RUTF), stimulation, follow-up.
- **Xerophthalmia**: XN night blindness → X1A → X1B Bitot's → X2 → X3A/X3B keratomalacia → XS → XF.
- Childhood obesity: BMI-for-age > +2 SD (5–19 y).

## 6. Therapeutic diets
- Modified normal diet — **consistency** (clear liquid → full liquid → soft → normal), **nutrients**, **meal pattern**.
- **If the gut works, use it**: oral → enteral (NG, gastrostomy) → parenteral.
- **NG feeding**: upright, **confirm tube position every time**, slow feed, flush before and after, upright 30–60 min after.
- **Obesity**: −500 kcal/day, high fibre, low fat, exercise; Indian BMI obese ≥ 25, waist ≥ 90 (M) / 80 (F).
- **Diabetes**: complex, low-GI carbohydrate, high fibre, no sugar, regular meals timed with medicines.
- **CVD**: less saturated/trans fat, salt < 5 g, DASH pattern, high fibre.
- **CKD**: limited protein (more if on dialysis), restrict Na, K (leaching), P, fluid (urine + ~500 ml).
- **Liver**: hepatitis — high CHO, adequate protein; cirrhosis — adequate protein, late evening snack, low salt for ascites, no alcohol.
- **Diarrhoea**: ORS, continue feeding/breastfeeding, zinc (children), extra meal after recovery. **Constipation**: fibre + fluids + activity.
- **Post-op**: early feeding; clear → full → soft → normal; high protein, vitamin C, zinc.

## 7. Cookery and food safety
- Pressure cooking/steaming save nutrients. Wash before cutting; big pieces; minimum water; cover; no soda; don't discard cooking water; don't overcook or reheat.
- Germination ↑ vitamin C; fermentation ↑ B vitamins; parboiling saves thiamine.
- Danger zone **5–60 °C**; cooked food not over 2 h at room temperature. Pasteurisation: 63 °C/30 min or 72 °C/15 s.
- Adulteration: metanil yellow (HCl → pink); papaya seeds in pepper (float in spirit); argemone → **epidemic dropsy**; khesari → **lathyrism**; starch in milk (iodine → blue).
- **PFA Act 1954 → FSSA 2006 (in force 2011), FSSAI**. AGMARK, ISI (BIS), "+F" logo.
- **WHO five keys**: keep clean; separate raw and cooked; cook thoroughly; safe temperatures; safe water and raw materials.

## 8. Assessment and programmes
- **ABCD**: anthropometry, biochemical, clinical, dietary (24-h recall, **FFQ**, diary, weighment).
- MUAC: midpoint of left upper arm. BMI = kg/m²; Indian: 18.5–22.9 normal, 23–24.9 overweight, ≥ 25 obese.
- Nutrition education: know the people, simple local messages, demonstration, participation, evaluation.
- **National Nutrition Policy 1993**; NFSA 2013; **POSHAN Abhiyaan 2018** (Poshan 2.0).
- **ICDS** (2 Oct 1975, MWCD): 6 services — supplementary nutrition, pre-school education, nutrition and health education, immunisation, health check-up, referral.
- **AMB** (2018): 6 beneficiary groups × 6 interventions × 6 institutional mechanisms.
- **WIFS** (2012): adolescents 10–19, weekly supervised IFA, biannual deworming.
- **MDM** (1995) → **PM POSHAN** (2021): hot cooked meal, government and aided schools.
- **NGCP 1962 → NIDDCP 1992**: universal iodised salt, monitoring, education.
- **Vitamin A**: 9 months–5 years, with MR vaccine then every 6 months (dose per NHM schedule).
- Nurse's role: identify, assess, deliver, educate, coordinate, record, evaluate.

questions.answer:
1. Nutrition: the science of food and its relationship to health — how food is eaten, digested, absorbed, used and its waste removed, together with the social and economic factors that decide what people eat.
2. Malnutrition: faulty nutrition — intake of nutrients not matching the body's needs.
3. Types: (a) under-nutrition — too little energy/protein for a long time (wasting, stunting, underweight); (b) over-nutrition — excess energy leading to overweight, obesity and diet-related diseases; (c) imbalance — wrong proportion of nutrients; (d) specific deficiency — lack of one nutrient (iodine → goitre, vitamin A → night blindness).
4. India has a double burden: under- and over-nutrition together.
5. Causes: poverty and food insecurity; large family, poor birth spacing; ignorance and food taboos; poor breastfeeding and complementary feeding; repeated infections and worms; poor water and sanitation; low status and education of women; for over-nutrition — energy-dense fast food, sedentary life.
6. Role of nutrition in health: supplies energy; builds and repairs tissues; regulates body processes (enzymes, hormones, fluid balance); protects against infection (breaks the malnutrition–infection cycle); prevents deficiency diseases; lowers risk of chronic diseases; supports learning, mental health and work capacity; speeds recovery after illness and surgery.
7. Diagram: malnutrition–infection cycle (poor intake → low immunity → infection → loss of appetite and nutrients → poorer intake).
8. Nurse's role: assess weight and BMI/MUAC, find the cause of poor intake, educate on balanced, low-cost diets, hygiene and immunisation.
questions.question: Define nutrition and malnutrition. Describe the types and causes of malnutrition and explain the role of nutrition in maintaining health.

questions.answer:
1. Nutrients by amount needed: macronutrients (carbohydrate, protein, fat — grams; water) and micronutrients (vitamins, minerals — mg or µg).
2. By chemical nature: organic (carbohydrate, protein, fat, vitamins) and inorganic (minerals, water).
3. By function: energy-yielding (carbohydrate 4, protein 4, fat 9 kcal/g) and non-energy-yielding (vitamins, minerals, water, fibre).
4. Six classes: carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals, water (fibre often added).
5. Foods by origin: plant (cereals, pulses, vegetables, fruits, nuts, oils, sugar) and animal (milk, egg, meat, fish, ghee). Animal foods give complete protein, B12, haem iron; plant foods give fibre, carotene, vitamin C.
6. By predominant nutrient: carbohydrate-rich (cereals, tubers), protein-rich (pulses, milk, meat), fat-rich (oils, nuts), vitamin- and mineral-rich (vegetables, fruits).
7. By function: energy-giving (cereals, fats, sugar), body-building (milk, pulses, egg, meat), protective (vegetables, fruits, milk, egg).
8. Basic four food groups: cereals and millets; protein foods (pulses, milk, egg, meat, fish); vegetables and fruits; fats, oils and sugar. Five-group system separates pulses and milk/meat.
9. ICMR-NIN 'My Plate' idea: eat from several groups every day, about half the plate vegetables and fruits.
questions.question: Classify nutrients in different ways. Classify foods by origin, by function and by food groups, giving examples.

questions.answer:
1. Economic: income, food prices, purchasing power — poor families eat mostly cereals.
2. Agricultural/geographic: local crops, season, climate, storage.
3. Social and cultural: religion, caste, customs, taboos (e.g. avoiding foods in pregnancy).
4. Family: size, birth order, who eats first (women and girls last), mother's education.
5. Personal: age, sex, likes, appetite, activity, pregnancy/lactation.
6. Health: illness, infection, worms, drugs, teeth.
7. Knowledge and cooking practices: e.g. discarding cooking water.
8. Psychological: stress, depression.
9. Media, urbanisation, fast food.
10. Government programmes: ICDS, PM POSHAN, PDS.
questions.question: Explain the factors affecting food and nutrition.

questions.answer:
1. Gives energy for body functions and work.
2. Builds and repairs tissues — growth, pregnancy, wound healing.
3. Regulates body processes — enzymes, hormones, fluid and acid–base balance.
4. Protects against infection; breaks the malnutrition–infection cycle.
5. Prevents deficiency diseases (anaemia, goitre, rickets, night blindness).
6. Lowers risk of chronic diseases (hypertension, diabetes, heart disease).
7. Supports learning, mental health and work capacity.
8. Speeds recovery and shortens hospital stay.
questions.question: Explain the role of nutrition in maintaining health.

questions.answer:
1. Meaning: under-nutrition and over-nutrition existing together in the same country, community or even household.
2. Under-nutrition: stunted, wasted and underweight children; anaemia in children and women; micronutrient deficiencies.
3. Over-nutrition: rising overweight, obesity, type 2 diabetes, hypertension and heart disease, including in children.
4. Causes: poverty and food insecurity alongside urbanisation, energy-dense processed foods, low physical activity.
5. Consequences: two kinds of disease to manage; malnourished children who become obese adults are at high risk of diabetes.
6. Response: programmes for under-nutrition (ICDS, AMB) plus healthy diet and activity promotion (Eat Right India); nurses screen for both.
questions.question: Write a short note on the 'double burden of malnutrition' in India.

questions.answer:
1. About 60% of adult body weight (more in infants).
2. Medium for all chemical reactions; transports nutrients and wastes.
3. Regulates temperature by sweating; lubricates joints; protects organs.
4. Lost in urine, stool, sweat and breath.
5. Needs rise in fever, hot weather, heavy work, diarrhoea, vomiting, lactation.
6. Elderly have weak thirst and dehydrate easily; children dehydrate fast in diarrhoea.
7. Nurse: maintain intake-output chart, encourage fluids, ORS in diarrhoea, restrict only when ordered (kidney or heart failure).
questions.question: Write a short note on water as a nutrient.

questions.answer: Nutrition is the science of food and its relationship to health — how food is eaten, digested, absorbed, used by the body and its waste removed, along with the factors that decide food choice.
questions.question: Define nutrition.

questions.answer: Carbohydrate 4 kcal/g, protein 4 kcal/g and fat 9 kcal/g (alcohol also gives 7 kcal/g but is not a nutrient).
questions.question: Name the energy-yielding nutrients with their calorie values.

questions.answer: Macronutrients are needed in grams (carbohydrate, protein, fat); micronutrients are needed in milligrams or micrograms (vitamins such as vitamin A, minerals such as iron).
questions.question: Differentiate macronutrients and micronutrients with examples.

questions.answer:
1. Definition: nitrogen-containing compounds of amino acids joined by peptide bonds (C, H, O, N ~16%, S).
2. Classification by quality: complete/high biological value (egg, milk, meat, fish) and incomplete (cereals low in lysine, pulses low in methionine); by origin: animal and plant.
3. Essential amino acids (8): isoleucine, leucine, lysine, methionine, phenylalanine, threonine, tryptophan, valine; histidine for infants; arginine semi-essential.
4. Functions: growth; repair and wound healing; enzymes and hormones; antibodies; transport (haemoglobin, albumin, transferrin); fluid balance through plasma albumin (oedema when low); buffers; clotting factors; structure (collagen, keratin, muscle); energy 4 kcal/g when needed.
5. Sources: animal — egg, milk, curd, paneer, meat, fish; plant — pulses (20–25%), soybean (~40%), nuts, oilseeds, cereals (6–12%).
6. Requirement (ICMR-NIN 2020): RDA 0.83 g/kg/day (EAR 0.66); man 54 g, woman 45.7 g; pregnancy +9.5 g (2nd) and +22 g (3rd trimester); lactation +16.9 g (0–6 m), +13.2 g (6–12 m); about 1 g/kg for low-quality cereal diets.
7. Improving quality: combine cereals and pulses (rice + dal, idli, khichdi), add milk; cereal : legume : milk ≈ 3 : 1 : 2.5; germination and fermentation.
8. Needs rise in growth, pregnancy, lactation, fever, burns, surgery; restricted in CKD before dialysis.
9. Deficiency: growth failure, oedema, low immunity, poor healing, PEM.
questions.question: Describe the classification, functions, dietary sources and requirements of proteins. Add a note on essential amino acids and improving protein quality.

questions.answer:
1. Unit of energy: kilocalorie — heat to raise 1 kg water by 1 °C; 1 kcal = 4.184 kJ. Fuel values: CHO 4, protein 4, fat 9 kcal/g.
2. BMR: energy used at complete physical and mental rest, awake, lying, 12–14 h after a meal, at comfortable temperature, for vital functions (heart, breathing, kidneys, temperature, cell activity).
3. Measured by indirect calorimetry or estimated from equations; ICMR-NIN 2020 found Indian BMR lower than international predictions.
4. Factors raising BMR: large surface area, more lean mass, childhood/growth, male sex, hyperthyroidism, adrenaline/stress, fever (~13% per °C), pregnancy, lactation, cold climate, burns, sepsis, physical training, caffeine/nicotine.
5. Factors lowering BMR: old age, female sex, more fat, hypothyroidism, starvation/under-nutrition, sleep (~10%).
6. Total energy expenditure = BMR × physical activity level; components: BMR (60–70% in sedentary), physical activity, thermic effect of food, plus growth, pregnancy, lactation.
7. ICMR-NIN 2020: man 2110/2710/3470 kcal; woman 1660/2130/2720 kcal (sedentary/moderate/heavy); pregnancy +350; lactation +600 (0–6 m), +520 (7–12 m).
8. Energy balance: intake > output → weight gain; < output → weight loss.
9. Nursing: fever, burns and sepsis need extra calories; monitor weight.
questions.question: Define basal metabolic rate (BMR). Explain the factors affecting BMR and the components of daily energy requirement. Give the ICMR-NIN 2020 energy requirements of adults.

questions.answer:
1. Main energy source, 4 kcal/g; glucose fuels the brain and red cells.
2. Protein-sparing action.
3. Prevents ketosis (needed for complete fat oxidation).
4. Stored as glycogen in liver and muscle.
5. Fibre aids bowel movement, lowers cholesterol and glucose rise.
6. Lactose helps calcium absorption.
7. Part of nucleic acids, glycoproteins.
Sources: cereals and millets (rice, wheat, ragi, jowar), roots and tubers (potato, tapioca), pulses, sugar, jaggery, honey, fruits (banana, mango, dates), milk (lactose).
questions.question: Write the functions and dietary sources of carbohydrates.

questions.answer:
1. Saturated (ghee, butter, coconut and palm oil), monounsaturated (groundnut, mustard, rice bran oil), polyunsaturated — n-6 linoleic (sunflower, safflower) and n-3 alpha-linolenic (mustard, soybean, flaxseed, fish); trans fats (vanaspati, reheated oil, bakery).
2. Visible (oils, ghee) and invisible (nuts, milk, egg, meat) fats.
3. Functions: concentrated energy 9 kcal/g; energy store; carries vitamins A, D, E, K; essential fatty acids; insulation and protection of organs; satiety; flavour; cell membranes, steroid hormones, bile acids.
4. Requirement: visible fat 20–50 g/day (ICMR-NIN 2020), use a mix of oils, avoid reheated oil and trans fats.
questions.question: Classify fats and write their functions and sources.

questions.answer:
1. Monosaccharides: glucose, fructose, galactose.
2. Disaccharides: sucrose (glucose + fructose), lactose (glucose + galactose), maltose (glucose + glucose).
3. Oligosaccharides: raffinose, stachyose (pulses — flatulence).
4. Polysaccharides: starch (cereals, tubers), glycogen (animal), cellulose and other fibres.
5. In food: starches, sugars and cellulose. Cellulose is not digested by humans — it is dietary fibre that adds bulk to stool.
questions.question: Write a note on the classification of carbohydrates.

questions.answer:
1. EFAs: linoleic acid (n-6) and alpha-linolenic acid (n-3) cannot be made by the body.
2. Needed for cell membranes, brain and retina (DHA), prostaglandins, skin health.
3. Sources: vegetable oils (sunflower, soybean, mustard), nuts, flaxseed, green leafy vegetables, fish. ICMR-NIN 2020 advises about 6.6 g n-6 and 2.2 g n-3 PUFA daily.
4. Deficiency: dry rough scaly skin (phrynoderma), poor growth, poor wound healing.
5. Excess fat: obesity, high cholesterol, atherosclerosis and coronary heart disease, fatty liver, gall stones; trans fats raise LDL and lower HDL.
questions.question: Explain essential fatty acids and the effects of excess fat intake.

questions.answer: Isoleucine, leucine, lysine, methionine, phenylalanine, threonine, tryptophan and valine (histidine is also essential for infants).
questions.question: Name the eight essential amino acids.

questions.answer: 0.83 g/kg body weight per day (EAR 0.66 g/kg): about 54 g/day for a 65 kg man and 45.7 g/day for a 55 kg woman.
questions.question: What is the protein RDA for adults according to ICMR-NIN 2020?

questions.answer: Combining two incomplete proteins so each supplies the amino acid the other lacks — cereals (low lysine) with pulses (low methionine), e.g. rice with dal or idli.
questions.question: What is supplementary value of proteins?

questions.answer: The amount of heat needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of water by 1 °C (from 14.5 to 15.5 °C); 1 kcal = 4.184 kJ.
questions.question: Define kilocalorie.

questions.answer:
1. Vitamins: organic compounds needed in small amounts, not made by the body. Fat-soluble — A, D, E, K (stored, can be toxic); water-soluble — B complex (B1, B2, niacin, B6, pantothenic acid, folate, B12, biotin) and C (not stored, lost in cooking).
2. Vitamin A forms: retinol (animal foods), beta-carotene (plant provitamin).
3. Functions: forms rhodopsin for dim-light vision; maintains epithelium of eye, skin, respiratory, gut and urinary tracts; immunity (reduces severity of measles and diarrhoea); growth and bone development; reproduction; carotene antioxidant.
4. Sources: liver, fish liver oil, egg yolk, milk, butter, ghee; green leafy vegetables (spinach, amaranth, drumstick leaves), carrot, pumpkin, papaya, mango.
5. RDA (ICMR-NIN 2020): man 1000 µg, woman 840 µg per day.
6. Deficiency: night blindness (earliest), conjunctival xerosis, Bitot's spots, corneal xerosis, keratomalacia and blindness; dry rough skin; frequent infections, higher child deaths.
7. Excess: from supplements — headache, vomiting, liver damage, harm to the foetus.
8. Nurse's role: check eyes and ask about night blindness; give vitamin A to children 9 months–5 years as per programme schedule and record; teach cheap carotene foods cooked with a little oil; promote breastfeeding (colostrum), measles immunisation, deworming, kitchen gardens; refer corneal involvement urgently.
questions.question: Classify vitamins. Describe the functions, sources, requirement and deficiency of vitamin A, and the nurse's role in prevention of vitamin A deficiency.

questions.answer:
1. Functions: part of haemoglobin (oxygen transport) and myoglobin; cytochromes and enzymes of energy release; immunity and brain development.
2. Forms: haem iron (meat, liver, fish) well absorbed; non-haem iron (cereals, pulses, green leafy vegetables, jaggery) poorly absorbed.
3. Sources: liver, meat, fish, egg; amaranth, drumstick leaves, bathua, mint; garden cress seeds; ragi, bajra; pulses; jaggery, dates, dried fruits; double-fortified salt, fortified rice.
4. Absorption increased by vitamin C, meat/fish, body need, germination and fermentation; decreased by tea and coffee (tannins), phytates, oxalates, calcium supplements at the same time, antacids.
5. RDA (ICMR-NIN 2020): man 19 mg, woman 29 mg per day; higher in pregnancy.
6. Iron deficiency anaemia: commonest nutritional deficiency in India (NFHS-5: about two-thirds of young children, over half of women anaemic).
7. Causes: low intake, increased need, blood loss (menstruation, hookworm, piles), malaria, closely spaced pregnancies.
8. Signs: pallor, fatigue, breathlessness, palpitations, koilonychia, pica, poor concentration.
9. Management/prevention: Hb testing, IFA as per protocol, deworming, iron-rich diet with vitamin C, no tea with meals, cooking in iron vessels, Anemia Mukt Bharat.
questions.question: Describe the functions, dietary sources, factors affecting absorption and requirement of iron. Add a note on iron deficiency anaemia.

questions.answer:
1. Fat-soluble: A, D, E, K; water-soluble: B complex and C.
2. Fat-soluble need fat and bile for absorption; water-soluble absorbed directly.
3. Fat-soluble stored in liver and fat; water-soluble little storage (except B12).
4. Deficiency of fat-soluble develops slowly; water-soluble quickly.
5. Excess fat-soluble (A, D) can be toxic; excess water-soluble mostly excreted in urine.
6. Water-soluble lost by washing, boiling and discarding water; heat destroys C and B1.
7. Fat-soluble need not be eaten daily; water-soluble need regular intake.
questions.question: Differentiate fat-soluble and water-soluble vitamins.

questions.answer:
1. Collagen formation — wound healing, healthy gums, blood vessels.
2. Increases absorption of non-haem iron.
3. Antioxidant; immunity.
4. Sources: amla (richest common source), guava, citrus fruits, tomato, green leafy vegetables, sprouted pulses.
5. RDA (ICMR-NIN 2020): man 80 mg, woman 65 mg.
6. Deficiency: scurvy — bleeding swollen gums, perifollicular haemorrhages, poor wound healing, bone and joint pain, anaemia; infantile scurvy with painful legs.
7. Destroyed by heat, air and soda — eat raw or lightly cooked, add lemon after cooking.
questions.question: Write the functions, sources and deficiency of vitamin C.

questions.answer:
1. Bones and teeth (99% of body calcium).
2. Blood clotting; muscle contraction including the heart; nerve transmission; enzyme activation.
3. Absorption helped by vitamin D, lactose, protein; reduced by phytates, oxalates, excess fibre.
4. Sources: milk and milk products (best), ragi (richest cereal), sesame, green leafy vegetables, small fish with bones.
5. RDA (ICMR-NIN 2020): 1000 mg/day for adults.
6. Deficiency: rickets, osteomalacia, osteoporosis, tetany.
questions.question: Write the functions, sources and requirement of calcium.

questions.answer:
1. Needed to make thyroid hormones that control BMR, growth and brain development.
2. Sources: iodised salt (main source), sea fish; plant iodine depends on soil.
3. RDA (ICMR-NIN 2020): 150 µg/day for adults.
4. Deficiency: iodine deficiency disorders — goitre, hypothyroidism, cretinism, intellectual disability, abortions, stillbirths.
5. Goitrogens (cabbage, cauliflower, tapioca in large raw amounts) interfere.
6. Prevention: universal iodised salt (NIDDCP); store in closed container away from heat and moisture.
questions.question: Write a note on iodine.

questions.answer:
1. Increases absorption of calcium and phosphorus.
2. Mineralisation of bones and teeth; keeps blood calcium normal with parathyroid hormone.
3. Muscle function and immunity.
4. Sources: sunlight on skin (main), fish liver oil, oily fish, egg yolk, liver, fortified milk and oil.
5. RDA (ICMR-NIN 2020): 600 IU/day.
6. Deficiency: rickets (children), osteomalacia (adults); excess: hypercalcaemia, kidney stones.
questions.question: Write the functions and sources of vitamin D.

questions.answer: Vitamins A, D, E and K.
questions.question: Name the fat-soluble vitamins.

questions.answer: Foamy, cheesy, triangular white spots on the conjunctiva (usually lateral), a sign of vitamin A deficiency (X1B in the WHO classification).
questions.question: What are Bitot's spots?

questions.answer: Amla and guava; it is destroyed by heat (prolonged cooking) and by alkali such as baking soda (also by exposure to air).
questions.question: Name two foods rich in vitamin C and two factors that destroy it.

questions.answer: 19 mg/day for a sedentary adult man and 29 mg/day for a sedentary adult woman.
questions.question: What is the ICMR-NIN 2020 iron RDA for an adult man and woman?

questions.answer:
1. Definition: a diet with a variety of foods in amounts and proportions that meet all needs for energy and nutrients with a small safety margin.
2. Principles: adequacy; balance; variety (all food groups); moderation (salt, sugar, fat); calorie control; nutrient density; individualisation (age, activity, culture, budget); safety.
3. Steps: find age, sex, weight, activity, physiological state → look up ICMR-NIN requirements → decide portions per food group (food guide/exchanges) → distribute across meals → choose dishes suited to habits and budget → calculate nutritive value and adjust → check variety and cost.
4. Pregnancy needs: energy +350 kcal (2nd/3rd trimester); protein +9.5 g (2nd) and +22 g (3rd trimester); more iron, folate, calcium, iodine, vitamins.
5. Sample day: early morning milk + soaked almonds/roasted chana; breakfast vegetable paratha or idli-sambar + egg; mid-morning fruit (guava/orange); lunch rotis/rice, dal, green leafy vegetable, salad, curd; evening sprouts chaat or ragi laddoo; dinner rice/roti, dal or fish/chicken, vegetable; bedtime milk.
6. Advice: one extra meal; iodised salt; take IFA and calcium as advised; avoid alcohol and tobacco, limit tea; small frequent meals for nausea; fibre and water for constipation; no harmful taboos; monitor weight gain.
questions.question: Define balanced diet. Explain the principles and steps of planning a balanced diet. Plan a balanced diet for a pregnant woman.

questions.answer:
1. Diagnosis: Hb below 11 g/dL (WHO); mild 10–10.9, moderate 7–9.9, severe below 7 g/dL; Hb at first antenatal visit and repeated.
2. Signs: pallor of conjunctiva, tongue, palms, nails; fatigue, breathlessness, palpitations, oedema, koilonychia.
3. Causes: low iron, folate, B12 intake; increased demand; short birth intervals; worms; malaria; blood loss; tea with meals.
4. Risks: preterm birth, low birth weight, heart failure, poor tolerance of postpartum bleeding, maternal death.
5. Diet: iron-rich foods every meal — green leafy vegetables, garden cress seeds, ragi, bajra, pulses and sprouts, jaggery, dates, meat, liver, fish, egg; vitamin C with each meal (amla, guava, lemon); iron vessels; folate-rich foods; protein foods; no tea/coffee with meals.
6. Supplementation: under Anemia Mukt Bharat, prophylactic IFA daily from the second trimester for about 180 days in pregnancy and continued after delivery; treatment of anaemia and deworming as per national protocol (doses as per guideline).
7. Counselling: take after food/at bedtime; with water or lemon water, not tea, coffee or milk; separate from calcium; black stools harmless; manage constipation with fibre and water; complete the course; keep tablets away from children.
8. Nurse: test Hb, record, follow up, refer severe anaemia.
questions.question: Describe anaemia in pregnancy — diagnosis, dietary management, iron-folic acid supplementation and counselling.

questions.answer:
Uses: planning diets for individuals and institutions; planning food supply and nutrition policy; supplementary feeding programmes (ICDS, PM POSHAN); evaluating diet surveys (EAR preferred for this); food labelling and fortification; nutrition education.
Limitations: meant for healthy people only; based on reference weights (65 kg man, 55 kg woman); not an individual's exact need — set above most people's requirement; does not cover all nutrients; values revised over time; ignores cooking losses and bioavailability differences; ignores habits and cost.
questions.question: Explain the uses and limitations of RDA.

questions.answer:
1. Initiate breastfeeding within one hour of birth; give colostrum; no prelacteal feeds.
2. Exclusive breastfeeding for six months.
3. Complementary feeding from six months, adequate in amount, frequency, consistency and variety.
4. Continue breastfeeding to two years or beyond.
5. Responsive, hygienic feeding with bowl and spoon, not bottle.
6. Feed during and after illness; extra food after recovery.
7. Progression: 6–8 months mashed semi-solids 2–3 meals; 9–11 months chopped family food 3–4 meals + snacks; 12–24 months family food 3–4 meals + 1–2 snacks.
questions.question: Write the IYCF guidelines on breastfeeding and complementary feeding.

questions.answer:
1. Foods grouped into lists; one exchange of any food in a list gives about the same energy, carbohydrate, protein and fat.
2. Lists: cereals, pulses, milk, vegetables, fruits, fats, sugar.
3. Approximate values: cereal 30 g ≈ 100 kcal, 3 g protein; pulse 30 g ≈ 100 kcal, 6 g protein; toned milk 100 ml ≈ 70 kcal, 3 g protein; fat 5 g ≈ 45 kcal; sugar 5 g ≈ 20 kcal.
4. Swaps: 1 roti ↔ ½ cup cooked rice.
5. Uses: diabetic and weight-reduction diets, renal diets, variety and choice for patients, easy calorie counting.
questions.question: Write a note on the food exchange system.

questions.answer:
1. Definition: plant food components not digested by human enzymes.
2. Insoluble (cellulose, lignin — bran, whole grains, vegetables): adds bulk, prevents constipation.
3. Soluble (pectin, gums, beta-glucan — fruits, oats, pulses, methi seeds, isabgol): slows glucose absorption, lowers cholesterol.
4. Benefits: prevents constipation, piles, diverticular disease; better glucose and cholesterol control; satiety and weight control; healthy gut bacteria.
5. Excess: gas, bloating, reduced mineral absorption; increase slowly with water.
questions.question: Write a note on dietary fibre.

questions.answer:
1. Energy needs fall (lower BMR and activity); protein, calcium, vitamin D, B12 and fibre needs stay or rise.
2. Problems: poor teeth, reduced taste and smell, poor appetite, constipation, weak thirst, depression, chronic diseases, many medicines, low income.
3. Plan: soft, easily chewed foods; small frequent meals; milk, curd, dal, egg, paneer for protein; milk and ragi plus sunlight for calcium and vitamin D; fibre and plenty of fluids; less salt, sugar and fat; light dinner.
4. Nurse: check dentition, weight, fluid intake, loneliness; involve family.
questions.question: Explain the dietary needs and diet plan for the elderly.

questions.answer: A diet containing a variety of foods in such amounts and proportions that all needs for energy and nutrients are met, with a small margin of extra nutrients for short periods of low intake.
questions.question: Define balanced diet.

questions.answer: Pregnancy: +350 kcal/day (2nd and 3rd trimesters). Lactation: +600 kcal/day (0–6 months) and +520 kcal/day (7–12 months).
questions.question: What is the extra energy requirement in pregnancy and lactation (ICMR-NIN 2020)?

questions.answer: Nutrient in the food = (nutrient content per 100 g from the Indian Food Composition Tables × weight eaten in grams) ÷ 100; add values of all foods for the day.
questions.question: How is the nutritive value of a food calculated?

questions.answer:
1. Definition: a range of conditions due to lack of protein and energy in varying proportions, mainly in under-fives, worsened by infection.
2. Magnitude: NFHS-5 — 35.5% stunted, 19.3% wasted, 32.1% underweight under-fives.
3. Causes: inadequate intake; infections (diarrhoea, measles, worms); poor IYCF; low birth weight; food insecurity; poor sanitation; poverty, illiteracy, large family, low status of women.
4. Classification: Wellcome (60–80% with oedema kwashiorkor, without underweight; <60% with oedema marasmic kwashiorkor, without marasmus); IAP grades I–IV; WHO Z-scores — wasting, stunting, underweight; SAM = WFH < −3 SD, MUAC < 11.5 cm or bilateral pitting oedema.
5. Kwashiorkor vs marasmus (table): oedema present/absent; age 1–3 y / under 1 y; flaky paint dermatosis / loose dry skin; fatty liver / no; moon face / old-man face; apathetic, poor appetite / alert, hungry; low albumin / near normal.
6. Management of SAM: NRC for complicated cases; WHO ten steps — hypoglycaemia, hypothermia, dehydration (ReSoMal, slow), electrolytes, infection, micronutrients (iron only in rehabilitation), cautious feeding (F-75), catch-up growth (F-100/RUTF), sensory stimulation, follow-up.
7. Prevention: maternal nutrition, breastfeeding and complementary feeding, growth monitoring, ICDS supplementary nutrition, immunisation, deworming, ORS and zinc, safe water, birth spacing, nutrition education.
8. Nurse's role: screening (weight, height, MUAC, oedema), referral, feeding by the clock, warmth, monitoring, mother's education, follow-up with ASHA/AWW.
questions.question: Define protein energy malnutrition. Describe its causes, classification and the differences between kwashiorkor and marasmus. Explain the management and prevention of PEM and the nurse's role.

questions.answer:
1. Causes: low intake of vitamin A/carotene; low fat intake; malabsorption; infections (diarrhoea, measles); PEM; worms; no breastfeeding.
2. WHO classification: XN night blindness; X1A conjunctival xerosis; X1B Bitot's spots; X2 corneal xerosis; X3A ulceration/keratomalacia < 1/3 cornea; X3B ≥ 1/3; XS corneal scar; XF xerophthalmic fundus.
3. Other features: dry rough skin, poor growth, frequent infections, higher child deaths.
4. Management: vitamin A as per national treatment schedule on doctor's order; treat infection and PEM; antibiotic eye drops as ordered; protect the eye; vitamin A-rich diet.
5. Prevention short term: periodic vitamin A supplementation for 9 months–5 years (with MR vaccine, then six-monthly).
6. Medium term: fortification of oil and milk.
7. Long term: green leafy and yellow vegetables, fruits, milk, egg, cooked with a little oil; breastfeeding and colostrum; measles immunisation; deworming; kitchen gardens; nutrition education.
8. Nurse: eye screening, giving and recording doses, education, urgent referral of corneal lesions.
questions.question: Describe the causes, clinical features (WHO classification of xerophthalmia), management and prevention of vitamin A deficiency.

questions.answer:
Criteria (6–59 months): weight-for-height < −3 SD, or MUAC < 11.5 cm, or bilateral pitting oedema. MAM: WFH −3 to −2 SD or MUAC 11.5–12.5 cm.
Ten steps: 1 prevent/treat hypoglycaemia; 2 hypothermia; 3 dehydration (ReSoMal, slowly); 4 correct electrolytes (potassium, magnesium); 5 treat infection; 6 correct micronutrients (iron later); 7 cautious feeding with F-75; 8 catch-up growth with F-100/RUTF; 9 sensory stimulation and emotional support; 10 prepare for follow-up.
questions.question: Write the criteria for severe acute malnutrition (SAM) and the WHO ten steps of management.

questions.answer:
1. Cause: low iodine in soil and water, not using iodised salt, goitrogens.
2. Foetus: abortion, stillbirth, cretinism (dwarfism, intellectual disability, deaf-mutism).
3. Newborn: neonatal hypothyroidism.
4. Child: goitre, poor school performance, retarded growth.
5. Adult: goitre, hypothyroidism, low work capacity.
6. Prevention: universal iodised salt (NIDDCP), correct storage, monitoring, newborn screening.
7. Nurse: test salt with kit, detect goitre, educate.
questions.question: Write a note on iodine deficiency disorders.

questions.answer:
1. Causes: lack of sunlight, low vitamin D and calcium intake, malabsorption, liver/kidney disease.
2. Signs: delayed fontanelle closure, craniotabes, frontal bossing, rickety rosary, Harrison's sulcus, pigeon chest, widened wrists, bow legs or knock knees, delayed teething and walking, pot belly, muscle weakness.
3. Management: vitamin D and calcium as prescribed, sunlight, calcium-rich diet.
4. Prevention: daily sun exposure, milk, egg, fish, fortified foods, supplements for at-risk babies as advised.
questions.question: Describe rickets — causes, signs and prevention.

questions.answer:
1. Definition: BMI-for-age > +1 SD overweight, > +2 SD obese (5–19 years); WFH > +2 SD/ +3 SD under five.
2. Causes: junk food, sugary drinks, inactivity, screen time, poor sleep, family history.
3. Signs: excess weight, abdominal fat, acanthosis nigricans, breathlessness, snoring, joint pain, low self-esteem.
4. Complications: type 2 diabetes, hypertension, fatty liver, adult obesity.
5. Management: family-based, no crash diet, regular meals, more vegetables, fruits, pulses, water not sugary drinks, ≥ 1 hour active play, limit screens.
6. Nurse: school screening, plotting BMI-for-age, counselling, referral.
questions.question: Write a note on childhood obesity and the nurse's role.

questions.answer:
Beriberi (thiamine B1): polished rice, over-washing rice, alcoholism; dry beriberi — peripheral neuritis, calf tenderness, foot drop; wet beriberi — oedema, heart failure; infantile beriberi; Wernicke's in alcoholics. Prevention: parboiled/unpolished rice, whole grains, pulses.
Pellagra (niacin): maize- or jowar-based diets, alcoholism; 4 D's — dermatitis (Casal's necklace on sun-exposed skin), diarrhoea, dementia, death. Prevention: groundnut, pulses, meat, milk, varied cereals.
questions.question: Write short notes on beriberi and pellagra.

questions.answer: Kwashiorkor has oedema and fatty liver (child apathetic, poor appetite); marasmus has severe wasting without oedema (child alert and hungry).
questions.question: Give two differences between kwashiorkor and marasmus.

1. Purpose of cooking: digestibility, safety, taste, destroying anti-nutrients, variety, keeping quality; cost — loss of vitamin C, B vitamins, minerals.
2. Moist heat: boiling (simple, safe, soft; water-soluble vitamins lost if water discarded); steaming (good retention, no fat; slower); pressure cooking (fast, saves fuel, good retention, tenderises pulses; risk if faulty, overcooking); stewing/simmering (liquid eaten; long time); poaching.
3. Dry heat: baking (flavour; thiamine and lysine loss); roasting (no fat, tasty; thiamine loss, burning); grilling (little fat; charring).
4. Frying: shallow and deep (tasty, quick, energy; high fat and calories, reheated oil forms harmful compounds, vitamin loss).
5. Microwave (quick, good retention; uneven heating) and solar cooking.
6. Prevention of loss: buy fresh, store properly; wash before cutting; cut large pieces just before cooking; peel thinly; don't over-wash rice and dal; minimum water, covered vessel; don't discard cooking water — use in soups/dal, absorption method for rice; add vegetables to boiling water; don't overcook or reheat; no baking soda; add lemon after cooking; don't reuse frying oil; iron vessels.

2. Types: intentional, incidental (pesticide residues, insect matter), metallic (lead, arsenic).
3. Examples: milk — water (lactometer), starch (iodine → blue); turmeric/dal — metanil yellow (HCl → pink); black pepper — papaya seeds (float in spirit); chilli powder — brick powder (sinks, gritty); mustard — argemone seeds/oil (epidemic dropsy); arhar dal — khesari dal (lathyrism); sugar/salt — chalk (settles); tea — used coloured leaves; peas/vegetables — malachite green (comes off on wet cotton).
4. Hazards: food poisoning, epidemic dropsy, lathyrism, cancer risk from non-permitted colours, liver and kidney damage, nutrient loss.
5. PFA Act 1954: defined adulteration; food standards; Central Food Laboratory, public analysts, food inspectors to take samples; penalties.
6. Replaced by Food Safety and Standards Act 2006 (in force 2011): single food law; set up FSSAI under MoHFW; science-based standards; licensing/registration of food businesses; limits for additives and contaminants; food safety officers and labs; labelling rules; penalties; Eat Right India, '+F' logo.

units.markdown:
# Unit 1: Introduction to nutrition, nutrients and foods

INC Unit I (2 hours): the basic ideas of nutrition and health, malnutrition, the role of nutrition in health, the factors that affect food and nutrition, the classification of nutrients and the classification of foods. Every later unit builds on the words defined here, so learn the definitions exactly.

## 1.1 Basic terms

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Food** | Anything eaten or drunk that nourishes the body: it gives energy, builds and repairs tissues, or regulates body processes. |
| **Nutrition** | The science of food and its relationship to health: how food is eaten, digested, absorbed, transported, used and how waste is removed, together with the social, economic and cultural factors that decide what people eat. |
| **Nutrient** | A chemical substance in food that the body needs for energy, growth, repair or regulation (carbohydrate, protein, fat, vitamins, minerals, water). |
| **Health** (WHO) | A state of complete physical, mental and social well-being and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity. |
| **Dietetics** | The application of nutrition science to plan and give diets to healthy and sick people. |
| **Diet** | The food and drink a person usually takes. |
| **Balanced diet** | A diet with all nutrients in the right amounts and proportions to meet the needs of the body, with a small extra margin for short periods of low intake (details in Unit 4). |
| **Optimum (good) nutrition** | All nutrients are supplied in amounts that meet the body's needs and allow normal growth, work and resistance to disease. |
| **Nutritional status** | The condition of the body as a result of the intake, absorption and use of nutrients; measured by nutritional assessment (Unit 8). |
| **Therapeutic diet** | A normal diet changed in consistency, nutrients or feeding pattern to treat or support treatment of a disease (Unit 6). |

## 1.2 Malnutrition

**Malnutrition** means faulty nutrition — any condition in which the intake of nutrients is not right for the body's needs. It has two sides.

```text
                         MALNUTRITION
                 ┌─────────────┴──────────────┐
          UNDER-NUTRITION               OVER-NUTRITION
   (too little energy or nutrients)   (too much energy or a nutrient)
   • Protein energy malnutrition      • Overweight and obesity
     (wasting, stunting,              • Diet-related non-communicable
      underweight)                      diseases (type 2 diabetes,
   • Micronutrient deficiencies         hypertension, heart disease)
     (iron, iodine, vitamin A,        • Excess of a single nutrient
      vitamin D, B vitamins)            (e.g. too much salt; too much
                                        vitamin A or D from supplements)
```

Four forms are often described:

1. **Under-nutrition** — not enough food for a long time (calories and protein).
2. **Over-nutrition** — eating too much, especially energy-dense foods, for a long time.
3. **Imbalance** — wrong proportion of nutrients even when the total amount is enough (e.g. plenty of rice but very little pulse, vegetable or milk).
4. **Specific deficiency** — lack of one nutrient, e.g. iodine (goitre), vitamin A (night blindness).

**The "double burden" of malnutrition.** India now has under-nutrition (stunted, wasted and anaemic children and women) and over-nutrition (obesity, diabetes) in the same country, sometimes in the same household. Nurses meet both.

**Causes of malnutrition (short list)** — poverty and food insecurity; large family and poor spacing of births; lack of knowledge of what to feed; wrong beliefs and food taboos; repeated infections (diarrhoea, worms, measles); poor sanitation and unsafe water; low status of women; early marriage and pregnancy; sedentary life and fast food for over-nutrition.

**Effects** — poor growth and learning in children, low birth weight babies, lower working capacity and income in adults, lowered immunity and more infections, higher maternal and child deaths, and chronic disease in later life.

## 1.3 Role of nutrition in maintaining health

Good nutrition:

- **Supplies energy** for body functions (breathing, heartbeat, temperature) and for work.
- **Builds and repairs** tissues — growth in childhood, pregnancy and lactation; wound healing after surgery.
- **Regulates** body processes — enzymes, hormones, fluid and acid–base balance, nerve and muscle function (vitamins, minerals, water).
- **Protects** against infection — well-fed people have better immunity; under-nourished children get more frequent and more severe infections, which further worsen nutrition (the malnutrition–infection cycle).
- **Prevents deficiency diseases** — anaemia, goitre, rickets, night blindness, scurvy.
- **Reduces the risk of chronic disease** — a diet low in salt, sugar and saturated fat, with enough fibre, vegetables and fruit, lowers the risk of hypertension, diabetes, heart disease and some cancers.
- **Supports mental health and working capacity** — iron and iodine deficiency reduce learning and work output.
- **Speeds recovery** — correct nutrition shortens hospital stay and reduces complications such as pressure ulcers and infection.

```text
THE MALNUTRITION–INFECTION CYCLE
 Inadequate intake → weight loss, low immunity, damaged gut lining
        ↑                                          ↓
 Loss of appetite, nutrient loss,      More frequent, longer, more
 higher needs during fever  ←──────── severe infections (diarrhoea,
                                       measles, pneumonia)
```

## 1.4 Factors affecting food and nutrition

| Group | Factors | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Economic | Income, food prices, purchasing power, employment | A poor family buys cereals but cannot afford milk, pulses, fruit |
| Agricultural / geographic | What grows locally, season, climate, storage facilities | Seasonal shortage of vegetables in some regions |
| Social and cultural | Religion, caste, customs, food habits, taboos | Avoiding certain foods in pregnancy or after delivery |
| Family | Family size, birth order, who eats first, mother's education | Women and girls eating last and least |
| Personal | Age, sex, likes and dislikes, appetite, activity, physiological state (pregnancy, lactation) | Elderly with poor teeth eat less protein |
| Health | Illness, infections, worms, drugs that change appetite or absorption, oral problems | Diarrhoea reduces absorption |
| Knowledge | Nutrition awareness, cooking methods | Washing rice too much, throwing away cooking water |
| Psychological | Stress, depression, emotional eating | Depression reduces appetite; stress eating causes weight gain |
| Media and urbanisation | Advertising, fast food, eating out, working hours | More packaged and fried snacks |
| Government programmes | ICDS, PM POSHAN, public distribution system | Hot cooked meals for school children |

## 1.5 Classification of nutrients

There are about 40–50 nutrients. They are classified in three common ways.

**A. By the amount needed**

| Macronutrients (needed in grams) | Micronutrients (needed in milligrams or micrograms) |
| --- | --- |
| Carbohydrates | Vitamins (fat soluble A, D, E, K; water soluble B group and C) |
| Proteins | Minerals (major: calcium, phosphorus, sodium, potassium, magnesium; trace: iron, iodine, zinc, copper, fluorine, selenium and others) |
| Fats | |
| (Water is also needed in large amounts) | |

**B. By chemical nature**

| Organic (contain carbon) | Inorganic (no carbon) |
| --- | --- |
| Carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins | Minerals, water |

**C. By function**

| Energy-yielding | Non-energy-yielding |
| --- | --- |
| Carbohydrate (4 kcal/g), protein (4 kcal/g), fat (9 kcal/g) | Vitamins, minerals, water, dietary fibre (fibre gives little usable energy) |

Another useful functional grouping:

- **Energy-giving foods**: cereals, roots and tubers, sugar, fats and oils.
- **Body-building foods**: milk, meat, fish, egg, pulses, nuts.
- **Protective foods**: vitamins and minerals — green leafy vegetables, other vegetables, fruits, milk, egg.

**Six classes of nutrients** (a common exam phrase): carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals and water. Dietary fibre is often added as a seventh dietary component.

## 1.6 Classification of foods

**A. By origin**

- **Plant (vegetable) origin**: cereals, millets, pulses, nuts and oilseeds, vegetables, fruits, sugar, vegetable oils, spices.
- **Animal origin**: milk and milk products, eggs, meat, fish, poultry, ghee and butter.

Animal foods generally give complete (high biological value) protein, vitamin B12, haem iron and retinol; plant foods give fibre, carotenes, vitamin C, folate and many minerals.

**B. By chemical composition (predominant nutrient)**

- Carbohydrate-rich: cereals, tubers, sugar.
- Protein-rich: pulses, milk, egg, meat, fish.
- Fat-rich: oils, ghee, butter, nuts.
- Vitamin- and mineral-rich: vegetables and fruits.

**C. By function** — energy-giving, body-building and protective (above).

**D. By food groups.** Food groups help in planning a balanced diet. Two common systems are used in Indian textbooks:

| Basic four food groups (Unit 4) | Five food groups (ICMR style) |
| --- | --- |
| 1. Cereals and millets (with roots and tubers) | 1. Cereals, millets and their products |
| 2. Pulses, legumes, milk, egg, meat, fish (protein foods) | 2. Pulses and legumes |
| 3. Vegetables and fruits | 3. Milk and meat products |
| 4. Fats, oils and sugars | 4. Fruits and vegetables |
| | 5. Fats and sugars |

The newer ICMR-NIN dietary guidance (the "My Plate for the Day" idea) asks people to eat from several food groups every day — cereals and millets, pulses, milk or curd, vegetables including green leafy vegetables, fruits, and nuts and seeds — rather than mostly cereals. Check the current ICMR-NIN Dietary Guidelines for Indians for the exact plate proportions.

**E. By nutritive value:** cereals and millets, pulses, nuts and oilseeds, vegetables (green leafy, roots and tubers, other vegetables), fruits, animal foods, fats and oils, sugar and jaggery, condiments and spices.

## 1.7 Water

Water forms about 60% of adult body weight (more in infants). It is the medium for all chemical reactions, transports nutrients and wastes, regulates body temperature by sweating, lubricates joints and protects organs. It is lost in urine, stool, sweat and breath. Needs rise in fever, hot weather, heavy work, diarrhoea and vomiting, and lactation. Thirst is weak in the elderly, so they become dehydrated easily.

## 1.8 Nursing application

- Use simple words with patients: "energy foods", "body-building foods", "protective foods".
- Look for both under- and over-nutrition at every admission (weight, height, BMI, MUAC in children).
- Find the reason behind poor intake: money, beliefs, teeth, depression, drugs, nausea.
- Respect religious and cultural food choices; suggest local, affordable substitutes (e.g. pulses and groundnuts instead of meat).
- Break the malnutrition–infection cycle: hand washing, safe water, immunisation and continued feeding during illness.

## Remember

- Nutrition = science of food and its relation to health; nutrient = chemical in food the body needs.
- Malnutrition = under-nutrition + over-nutrition + imbalance + specific deficiency.
- Macronutrients: carbohydrate, protein, fat; micronutrients: vitamins, minerals.
- Organic: carbohydrate, protein, fat, vitamins; inorganic: minerals, water.
- Energy: carbohydrate 4, protein 4, fat 9 kcal per gram.
- Foods by function: energy-giving, body-building, protective.
- Basic four food groups: cereals; protein foods (pulses, milk, egg, meat); vegetables and fruits; fats, oils and sugar.
- India has a double burden of malnutrition.

# Unit 2: Carbohydrates, energy, proteins and fats

This notes file joins three small INC units: **Unit II** Carbohydrates and Energy (3 hours), **Unit III** Proteins (3 hours) and **Unit IV** Fats (2 hours). These are the three energy-yielding macronutrients. For each one learn: composition/classification, functions, dietary sources and requirement (RDA).

Requirement figures below are from the **ICMR-NIN 2020 report "Nutrient Requirements for Indians — Recommended Dietary Allowances (RDA) and Estimated Average Requirements (EAR)"** and its official brief note. Reference adults: man 65 kg, woman 55 kg.

## 2.1 RDA and EAR — two words you need first

- **EAR (Estimated Average Requirement)**: the median requirement of healthy people of a group — the intake that meets the need of half of them.
- **RDA (Recommended Dietary Allowance)**: a higher value, at the upper end of the distribution of requirements, that meets the needs of nearly all healthy people of the group.
- The 2020 committee advises using the **EAR** for judging the adequacy of a population's diet and for diet planning, and the **RDA** as a safe target. It also introduced **tolerable upper limits (TUL)** because many foods are now fortified.
- EAR is roughly 80% of the RDA.

## 2.2 Carbohydrates

**Definition.** Organic compounds of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen (usually H : O = 2 : 1); chemically, polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones and the substances that give them on hydrolysis. They are the cheapest and main source of energy in the Indian diet.

### Composition and classification

| Class | Units | Examples and sources |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Monosaccharides** (simple sugars) | 1 sugar unit | Glucose (fruits, honey), fructose (fruits, honey), galactose (from milk lactose) |
| **Disaccharides** | 2 units | Sucrose = glucose + fructose (table sugar, jaggery); lactose = glucose + galactose (milk); maltose = glucose + glucose (germinating grains, malt) |
| **Oligosaccharides** | 3–10 units | Raffinose, stachyose in pulses (cause flatulence) |
| **Polysaccharides** | many units | **Starch** (cereals, millets, potato, tubers); **glycogen** (animal starch, stored in liver and muscle); **cellulose** and other fibres (vegetables, fruits, whole grains, bran) |

The INC syllabus describes carbohydrates in food as **starches, sugars and cellulose**:

- **Starch** — the main storage carbohydrate of plants; digested by salivary and pancreatic amylase to maltose and then glucose. Cooking makes starch granules swell and burst so it is digested better.
- **Sugars** — mono- and disaccharides; sweet, quickly absorbed; excess gives "empty calories" and dental caries.
- **Cellulose** — a polysaccharide of glucose that human enzymes cannot digest; part of **dietary fibre**. It adds bulk to stool.

**Dietary fibre** (more in Unit 4): soluble fibre (pectin, gums in fruits, oats, pulses) lowers blood cholesterol and slows glucose absorption; insoluble fibre (cellulose, lignin in bran, whole grains, vegetables) adds bulk and prevents constipation.

### Functions of carbohydrates

1. **Main source of energy** — 4 kcal per gram; glucose is the preferred fuel of the brain and the only fuel of red blood cells.
2. **Protein-sparing action** — enough carbohydrate lets protein be used for growth and repair instead of being burnt for energy.
3. **Prevents ketosis** — some carbohydrate is needed for complete fat oxidation; on starvation or very low-carbohydrate diets ketone bodies accumulate.
4. **Stored as glycogen** in liver (keeps blood glucose normal between meals) and muscle (fuel for exercise).
5. **Fibre** helps bowel movement and lowers cholesterol and the glycaemic response.
6. **Lactose** helps calcium absorption and favours useful gut bacteria.
7. **Structural parts** of compounds such as nucleic acids (ribose), glycoproteins and glycolipids.
8. Gives **taste and variety** to food.

### Dietary sources

- **Cereals and millets**: rice, wheat, maize, jowar, bajra, ragi — about 65–75% carbohydrate.
- **Roots and tubers**: potato, sweet potato, tapioca, yam.
- **Pulses**: about half their weight is carbohydrate besides protein.
- **Sugars**: sugar, jaggery, honey, sweets, soft drinks.
- **Fruits**: banana, mango, dates, grapes; dried fruits.
- **Milk**: lactose.

### Requirement

ICMR-NIN gives requirements for **energy** and protein; carbohydrate makes up the energy left after protein and fat, so it supplies most of the day's calories in the usual Indian diet. ICMR-NIN advises getting carbohydrate mainly from whole grains, millets, pulses, vegetables and fruits and limiting refined sugar; WHO advises keeping free (added) sugars below 10% of daily energy. A diet with too much polished cereal and sugar and too little pulse, vegetable and milk is unbalanced even when it gives enough calories.

## 2.3 Energy

**Unit of energy.** The **kilocalorie (kcal)** — the heat needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of water by 1 °C (from 14.5 to 15.5 °C). The international unit is the **kilojoule**: 1 kcal = 4.184 kJ.

**Energy value of foods (physiological fuel values):**

| Nutrient | kcal per gram |
| --- | --- |
| Carbohydrate | 4 |
| Protein | 4 |
| Fat | 9 |
| Alcohol | 7 (no nutrients — "empty calories") |

Example: a snack with 20 g carbohydrate, 5 g protein and 10 g fat = (20 × 4) + (5 × 4) + (10 × 9) = 80 + 20 + 90 = **190 kcal**.

### Total energy expenditure

The day's energy need = **BMR × PAL** (physical activity level). It has three parts:

1. **Basal metabolic rate** — the largest part (about 60–70% in sedentary people).
2. **Physical activity** — the most variable part.
3. **Thermic effect of food (specific dynamic action)** — energy used to digest, absorb and process food; highest for protein.
4. Plus extra for **growth** in children, **pregnancy** and **lactation**.

### Basal metabolic rate (BMR)

**Definition.** The energy the body uses at complete physical and mental rest to keep vital functions going — heartbeat, breathing, kidney work, nerve activity, body temperature and cell activity. It is measured in the morning, 12–14 hours after the last meal, lying awake and relaxed, at a comfortable room temperature (thermoneutral).

**Measurement**: by indirect calorimetry (oxygen used and carbon dioxide produced), or estimated from equations using weight, age and sex. ICMR-NIN 2020 noted that Indians have lower BMR than predicted from international equations (more body fat, less muscle) and reduced the adult estimate.

### Factors affecting BMR

| Factor | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| **Body surface area and size** | Larger surface area → higher BMR |
| **Body composition** | More lean (muscle) tissue → higher BMR; more fat → lower |
| **Age** | Highest in infancy and childhood (growth); falls with age |
| **Sex** | Men have higher BMR than women (more lean mass) |
| **Thyroid hormones** | Hyperthyroidism raises BMR markedly; hypothyroidism lowers it |
| **Other hormones** | Adrenaline (stress, fear) raises it; growth hormone, testosterone raise it |
| **Fever** | Each 1 °C rise raises BMR by about 13% |
| **Pregnancy and lactation** | Raised |
| **Climate** | Higher in cold climates |
| **Starvation and under-nutrition** | Lowered (the body saves energy) |
| **Sleep** | About 10% lower during sleep |
| **Drugs and stimulants** | Caffeine and nicotine raise it slightly |
| **Physical training** | Raises it through more muscle |
| **Disease** | Burns, trauma, sepsis raise it greatly |

### Energy requirement (ICMR-NIN 2020)

| Group | Energy (kcal/day) |
| --- | --- |
| Adult man, sedentary / moderate / heavy work | 2110 / 2710 / 3470 |
| Adult woman, sedentary / moderate / heavy work | 1660 / 2130 / 2720 |
| Pregnancy (2nd and 3rd trimester, over the woman's need) | + 350 |
| Lactation 0–6 months / 7–12 months | + 600 / + 520 |
| Infants 0–6 months / 6–12 months | 530 / 660 |

Children's and adolescents' figures are in Unit 4. The 2020 values for adults are lower than the 2010 values because Indians were found to spend less energy for the same activities and to have lower BMR.

**Energy balance**: intake = expenditure → weight steady; intake > expenditure → weight gain (stored as fat); intake < expenditure → weight loss.

## 2.4 Proteins

**Definition.** Complex nitrogen-containing organic compounds made of **amino acids** joined by peptide bonds. They contain carbon, hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen (about 16% nitrogen), often sulphur and sometimes phosphorus. The word comes from Greek "proteios" — of first importance.

### Composition

About 20 amino acids are found in body proteins. They are grouped by whether the body can make them.

| Essential (indispensable) | Non-essential (dispensable) |
| --- | --- |
| Must come from food because the body cannot make them in enough amount | The body can make them from other substances |

**The eight essential amino acids** (as listed in the INC syllabus): **isoleucine, leucine, lysine, methionine, phenylalanine, threonine, tryptophan, valine**. **Histidine** is also essential for infants (and is now counted as essential for all ages, giving nine); **arginine** is semi-essential (needed during growth).

Memory aid: **"PVT TIM HALL"** — Phenylalanine, Valine, Threonine, Tryptophan, Isoleucine, Methionine, (Histidine, Arginine), Leucine, Lysine.

### Quality of protein

- **Complete protein (high biological value)**: has all essential amino acids in the right proportion — egg (reference protein), milk, meat, fish.
- **Incomplete protein**: short of one or more essential amino acids (the **limiting amino acid**). Cereals are low in **lysine**; pulses are low in **methionine** (sulphur amino acids).
- **Supplementary value (mutual supplementation)**: combining cereals and pulses corrects both shortages — e.g. rice + dal, idli, dosa, khichdi, chapati + dal. Adding a little milk improves it further. ICMR-NIN 2020 advises a cereal : legume : milk ratio of about **3 : 1 : 2.5** for good protein quality.
- Measures of protein quality: biological value (BV), net protein utilisation (NPU), protein efficiency ratio (PER), amino acid score; the 2020 report introduced **DIAAS** (digestible indispensable amino acid score).

### Functions of proteins

1. **Growth and building of new tissue** — infancy, childhood, adolescence, pregnancy, lactation.
2. **Repair and maintenance** — wound healing, recovery from surgery, burns and illness; replacing worn-out cells.
3. **Enzymes** (amylase, pepsin), **hormones** (insulin, growth hormone) and **neurotransmitter** precursors (tryptophan → serotonin).
4. **Antibodies (immunoglobulins)** — defence against infection.
5. **Transport** — haemoglobin (oxygen), transferrin (iron), lipoproteins (fats), albumin (drugs, bilirubin).
6. **Fluid balance** — plasma albumin maintains oncotic pressure; low albumin causes oedema (as in kwashiorkor and liver disease).
7. **Acid–base balance** — proteins act as buffers.
8. **Blood clotting** — fibrinogen, prothrombin.
9. **Structure** — collagen (skin, bone, tendon), keratin (hair, nails), actin and myosin (muscle).
10. **Energy** — 4 kcal/g, used when carbohydrate and fat are not enough (wasteful).

### Dietary sources

| Animal (high quality) | Plant (lower quality alone, good when combined) |
| --- | --- |
| Egg, milk, curd, paneer, cheese | Pulses and legumes (20–25% protein) — dal, rajma, chana, moong |
| Meat, poultry, fish | Soybean (about 40% protein — the richest plant source) |
| | Nuts and oilseeds — groundnut, almonds, sesame |
| | Cereals and millets (about 6–12% protein) — eaten in large amounts, so they give much of the protein in Indian diets |

### Protein requirement (ICMR-NIN 2020)

| Group | EAR | RDA |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Healthy adults | 0.66 g/kg/day | **0.83 g/kg/day** |
| Adult man (65 kg) | 42.9 g/day | **54.0 g/day** |
| Adult woman (55 kg) | 36.3 g/day | **45.7 g/day** |
| Pregnancy, 2nd trimester (extra) | + 7.6 g | **+ 9.5 g** |
| Pregnancy, 3rd trimester (extra) | + 17.6 g | **+ 22.0 g** |
| Lactation 0–6 months (extra) | + 13.6 g | **+ 16.9 g** |
| Lactation 6–12 months (extra) | + 10.6 g | **+ 13.2 g** |

The report notes that people eating a cereal-based diet with low-quality protein need about **1 g/kg/day**. The 2010 RDA was 1 g/kg/day.

**Needs rise** in growth, pregnancy, lactation, fever, infection, burns, surgery, injury, fractures and recovery from malnutrition. **Protein is restricted** in some cases — advanced kidney failure not on dialysis and hepatic encephalopathy (Unit 6).

### Deficiency and excess

- Deficiency → poor growth, wasting, oedema, low immunity, poor wound healing, anaemia, fatty liver; in children protein energy malnutrition (Unit 5).
- Excess (very high protein for long periods) adds load on the kidneys and is costly; the extra is burnt for energy or stored as fat.

## 2.5 Fats (lipids)

**Definition.** Fats are esters of **fatty acids** with **glycerol** (triglycerides). Lipids are organic compounds insoluble in water but soluble in organic solvents. Fats are solid at room temperature; oils are liquid.

### Classification

**A. By saturation of fatty acids**

| Type | Bonds | Examples and sources | Effect on health |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Saturated fatty acids (SFA)** | No double bonds | Palmitic, stearic — ghee, butter, coconut oil, palm oil, meat fat | In excess raise LDL cholesterol |
| **Monounsaturated (MUFA)** | One double bond | Oleic acid — groundnut, mustard, rice bran, olive oil | Lower LDL; heart-friendly |
| **Polyunsaturated (PUFA)** | Two or more double bonds | **Linoleic acid (n-6)** — sunflower, safflower, soybean, corn oil; **alpha-linolenic acid (n-3)** — mustard, soybean, flaxseed, green leafy vegetables, fish (EPA, DHA) | Lower cholesterol; essential |
| **Trans fatty acids** | Formed when oils are partially hydrogenated or reheated many times | Vanaspati, bakery and fried snacks | Raise LDL and lower HDL — the most harmful |

**B. Other classifications**: visible fats (oil, ghee, butter added in cooking) and invisible fats (present inside foods — nuts, cereals, pulses, milk, egg, meat); simple lipids (fats, waxes), compound lipids (phospholipids, lipoproteins) and derived lipids (fatty acids, cholesterol, steroids).

**Essential fatty acids (EFA)**: linoleic acid (omega-6) and alpha-linolenic acid (omega-3) cannot be made by the body and must come from food. Their deficiency causes dry, rough, scaly skin (phrynoderma, "toad skin", is linked to it), poor growth and poor wound healing.

### Calorie value

Fat gives **9 kcal per gram** — more than twice carbohydrate or protein. This makes fat useful to raise energy in small volumes (for children and underweight patients) and a problem in obesity.

### Functions of fats

1. Concentrated **source of energy**; stored fat is the body's energy reserve.
2. **Carries fat-soluble vitamins** A, D, E and K and helps their absorption (carotene is absorbed better when cooked with a little oil).
3. Supplies **essential fatty acids** — needed for cell membranes, brain and retina (DHA), and for making prostaglandins.
4. **Insulation** — fat under the skin keeps the body warm.
5. **Protection** — fat pads around kidneys, heart and eyes protect them.
6. **Satiety** — fat slows stomach emptying, so meals keep you full longer.
7. **Taste and texture** of food.
8. **Structural** — phospholipids and cholesterol are part of every cell membrane; cholesterol forms bile acids, vitamin D and steroid hormones.

### Dietary sources

- **Visible fats**: cooking oils (groundnut, mustard, sunflower, rice bran, sesame, coconut, soybean), ghee, butter, vanaspati.
- **Invisible fats**: nuts and oilseeds, whole milk and milk products, egg yolk, meat, fish, and small amounts in cereals and pulses.
- **Cholesterol** is only in animal foods: egg yolk, organ meats, butter, ghee, full-cream milk. Plant oils have no cholesterol.

### Fat requirement (ICMR-NIN 2020)

- **Visible fat (cooking oil and ghee): 20–50 g per person per day** (about 4–10 teaspoons), depending on energy need, physical activity and physiological state. For a 2000 kcal diet, not more than about **27 g** of visible fat a day.
- Enough nuts, oilseeds and diverse foods to supply about **6.6 g of n-6 PUFA and 2.2 g of n-3 PUFA** a day.
- Use a **combination of oils** (e.g. groundnut or rice bran with mustard or soybean) rather than one oil, to balance the fatty acids; avoid reheating oil; limit vanaspati, bakery and fried foods (trans fats), and ghee and butter.

### Effects of excess and deficiency

- Excess: obesity, raised blood cholesterol, atherosclerosis and coronary heart disease, fatty liver, gall stones; some cancers.
- Deficiency: low energy intake and weight loss, deficiency of fat-soluble vitamins, essential fatty acid deficiency (dry rough skin, poor growth).

## 2.6 Comparing the three macronutrients

| Feature | Carbohydrate | Protein | Fat |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Elements | C, H, O | C, H, O, N (S, P) | C, H, O |
| Unit | Glucose (monosaccharides) | Amino acids | Fatty acids + glycerol |
| kcal/g | 4 | 4 | 9 |
| Main job | Energy | Growth and repair | Concentrated energy, fat-soluble vitamins |
| Storage in body | Glycogen (small) | No true store (muscle protein used in starvation) | Adipose tissue (large) |
| Key sources | Cereals, tubers, sugar | Pulses, milk, egg, meat, fish | Oils, ghee, nuts |
| Requirement basis | Rest of energy need | 0.83 g/kg/day (RDA) | Visible fat 20–50 g/day |

## 2.7 Nursing application

- Count calories in simple terms for patients: oil and fried snacks add many calories in a small volume.
- For an underweight or post-operative patient, raise energy and protein by adding milk, curd, egg, dal, groundnut and a little oil or ghee to small frequent meals.
- Teach cereal + pulse combinations to vegetarian families to improve protein quality cheaply.
- Fever, burns and sepsis raise BMR — plan more calories and protein and monitor weight.
- Teach heart-friendly fat use: mixed oils, no reheating, less vanaspati and bakery foods.

## Remember

- 1 kcal = 4.184 kJ; carbohydrate 4, protein 4, fat 9, alcohol 7 kcal/g.
- Carbohydrates = starches, sugars, cellulose; glucose is the brain's main fuel; carbohydrate spares protein and prevents ketosis.
- BMR: energy at complete rest; raised by thyroxine, fever (about 13% per °C), growth, pregnancy, cold, lean mass; lowered by starvation, old age, hypothyroidism, sleep.
- ICMR-NIN 2020 energy: man 2110/2710/3470; woman 1660/2130/2720 kcal (sedentary/moderate/heavy); pregnancy +350; lactation +600 then +520.
- Eight essential amino acids: isoleucine, leucine, lysine, methionine, phenylalanine, threonine, tryptophan, valine (+ histidine in infants).
- Cereals lack lysine, pulses lack methionine — combine them.
- Protein RDA 0.83 g/kg/day (EAR 0.66): man 54 g, woman 45.7 g; pregnancy +9.5 g (2nd) and +22 g (3rd trimester).
- Visible fat 20–50 g/day; EFAs = linoleic (n-6) and alpha-linolenic (n-3); trans fats are the worst.
