# Unit 3: Vitamins and minerals

This notes file joins **INC Unit V Vitamins** (3 hours) and **INC Unit VI Minerals** (3 hours). These are the micronutrients — needed in small amounts but essential. For each one learn the functions, dietary sources and requirement. Deficiency diseases are only listed here; their causes, signs, management and the nurse's role are in Unit 5.

**Requirement figures** in this file are the ICMR-NIN 2020 RDA for a **sedentary adult man (65 kg) and woman (55 kg)**, taken from the official ICMR-NIN 2020 brief note. B-vitamin needs rise with energy intake, so moderate and heavy workers, adolescents, pregnant and lactating women have different (mostly higher) values in the full report. Where the brief note gives no figure, no number is quoted here — look it up in the ICMR-NIN 2020 RDA report.

## 3.1 Vitamins — definition and classification

**Vitamins** are organic compounds needed in very small amounts for normal growth, metabolism and health. The body cannot make them (or makes too little), so they must come from food. They give no energy but many work as coenzymes in energy-releasing reactions.

| Fat-soluble vitamins | Water-soluble vitamins |
| --- | --- |
| A, D, E, K | B complex (B1 thiamine, B2 riboflavin, niacin, B6 pyridoxine, pantothenic acid, folic acid, B12, biotin) and C (ascorbic acid) |
| Absorbed with fat, need bile | Absorbed directly into blood |
| Stored in the liver and fat tissue | Little storage (except B12 in the liver) |
| Deficiency develops slowly | Deficiency develops quickly |
| Excess can be toxic (especially A and D from supplements) | Excess usually passed in urine |
| Not lost much in cooking water | Lost by washing, boiling and throwing water away, and by heat (C, B1) |
| Need not be eaten daily | Need regular intake |

## 3.2 Fat-soluble vitamins

### Vitamin A (retinol)

- **Forms**: preformed vitamin A (retinol) in animal foods; **provitamin A carotenoids (beta-carotene)** in plant foods, converted to retinol in the intestine.
- **Functions**: (1) **vision in dim light** — forms rhodopsin (visual purple) in the rods of the retina; (2) keeps the **epithelium** of the eye, skin, respiratory, gut and urinary tracts healthy and moist; (3) **immunity** — reduces severity of measles and diarrhoea; (4) growth and bone development; (5) reproduction; (6) beta-carotene is an antioxidant.
- **Sources**: animal — liver, fish liver oils, egg yolk, milk, butter, ghee; plant (carotene) — green leafy vegetables (spinach, amaranth, drumstick leaves, coriander, methi), yellow-orange vegetables and fruits (carrot, pumpkin, papaya, mango).
- **RDA (2020)**: man **1000 µg**, woman **840 µg** per day.
- **Deficiency**: night blindness, xerophthalmia (conjunctival and corneal xerosis, Bitot's spots, keratomalacia), dry rough skin, more infections (Unit 5). **Excess** (mostly from supplements): headache, vomiting, liver damage; can harm the unborn baby — a reason supplements are given only as prescribed.

### Vitamin D (calciferol)

- **Forms**: D3 (cholecalciferol) made in the skin by sunlight (ultraviolet B) and found in animal foods; D2 (ergocalciferol) from plants and yeast. Activated in the liver and then the kidney to calcitriol.
- **Functions**: increases **absorption of calcium and phosphorus** from the gut; helps mineralisation of bones and teeth; maintains blood calcium with parathyroid hormone; supports muscle function and immunity.
- **Sources**: **sunlight on bare skin** (main source); fish liver oils, oily fish, egg yolk, liver, fortified milk and oil.
- **RDA (2020)**: **600 IU** per day for adult men and women.
- **Deficiency**: **rickets** in children, **osteomalacia** in adults, contributes to osteoporosis. **Excess**: high blood calcium, kidney stones, calcification of soft tissues.

### Vitamin E (tocopherols)

- **Functions**: main **antioxidant** in cell membranes — protects PUFA and red cell membranes from damage by free radicals; supports immunity and nerve function.
- **Sources**: vegetable oils (sunflower, safflower, wheat germ), nuts and seeds, green leafy vegetables, whole grains.
- **Requirement**: linked to PUFA intake; see the full ICMR-NIN 2020 report.
- **Deficiency**: rare; haemolytic anaemia in premature infants; nerve and muscle problems in fat malabsorption.

### Vitamin K (phylloquinone, menaquinone)

- **Functions**: needed by the liver to make **clotting factors** (prothrombin, factors VII, IX, X); also for bone proteins.
- **Sources**: green leafy vegetables (spinach, cabbage, broccoli), vegetable oils; **gut bacteria** also make it.
- **Requirement**: see the full ICMR-NIN 2020 report.
- **Deficiency**: bleeding — **haemorrhagic disease of the newborn** (newborns have sterile guts and breast milk is low in vitamin K, which is why newborns receive vitamin K prophylaxis by protocol); bleeding in obstructive jaundice and long antibiotic use.

## 3.3 Water-soluble vitamins

| Vitamin | Main functions | Good sources | ICMR-NIN 2020 RDA (man / woman, sedentary) | Deficiency |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Thiamine (B1)** | Coenzyme in carbohydrate metabolism; nerve function | Whole grains, unpolished/parboiled rice, pulses, nuts, oilseeds, pork, yeast | 1.8 / 1.7 mg | **Beriberi** (dry — nerves; wet — heart failure, oedema), Wernicke's encephalopathy in alcohol use |
| **Riboflavin (B2)** | Coenzyme (FAD, FMN) in energy release; healthy skin, eyes | Milk, curd, egg, liver, green leafy vegetables, pulses | 2.5 / 2.4 mg | **Angular stomatitis**, cheilosis, glossitis (magenta tongue), seborrhoeic dermatitis |
| **Niacin (nicotinic acid)** | Coenzyme (NAD, NADP) in energy release; can be made from tryptophan | Groundnut, meat, fish, liver, whole cereals, pulses | 18 / 14 mg | **Pellagra** — the 3 D's: dermatitis, diarrhoea, dementia (death); seen with diets based on maize or jowar |
| **Pyridoxine (B6)** | Coenzyme in amino acid metabolism; haemoglobin and neurotransmitter synthesis | Cereals, pulses, meat, fish, vegetables | 2.4 / 1.9 mg | Peripheral neuritis, convulsions in infants, anaemia; deficiency can occur with long isoniazid use |
| **Pantothenic acid** | Part of coenzyme A — energy metabolism, fatty acid and hormone synthesis | Widespread in foods ("pantothen" = everywhere): liver, egg, whole grains, pulses | See full report | Very rare; "burning feet" syndrome |
| **Folic acid (folate)** | DNA synthesis and cell division; red cell formation; prevents **neural tube defects** | Green leafy vegetables, pulses, liver, groundnut | 300 / 220 µg (dietary folate equivalents) | **Megaloblastic anaemia**; neural tube defects in the baby if low before and in early pregnancy |
| **Vitamin B12 (cobalamin)** | DNA synthesis, red cell formation, myelin of nerves; needs intrinsic factor from the stomach for absorption | **Only animal foods**: milk, curd, egg, meat, fish, liver | 2.2 / 2.2 µg | **Megaloblastic anaemia**, pernicious anaemia, nerve damage; risk in strict vegetarians and the elderly |
| **Vitamin C (ascorbic acid)** | Collagen formation (wound healing, healthy gums and vessels); **increases iron absorption**; antioxidant; immunity | Amla (richest common source), guava, citrus fruits, tomato, green leafy vegetables, sprouted pulses | 80 / 65 mg | **Scurvy** — bleeding swollen gums, small skin bleeds, poor wound healing, bone pain |

Biotin is also a B vitamin (fat and glucose metabolism; sources egg yolk, liver, nuts; deficiency rare, linked with eating many raw egg whites).

**Losses in cooking**: vitamin C and thiamine are destroyed by heat, air and alkali (adding soda); all water-soluble vitamins leach into washing and cooking water. Unit 7 gives the measures to save them.

## 3.4 Minerals — definition and classification

**Minerals** are inorganic elements that remain as ash when food is burnt. They form about 4% of body weight.

| Major minerals (macrominerals) — needed more than 100 mg/day | Trace elements (microminerals) — needed in very small amounts |
| --- | --- |
| **Calcium, phosphorus, sodium, potassium, magnesium** (also chloride and sulphur) | Iron, iodine, zinc, copper, fluorine, selenium, manganese, chromium, cobalt (as part of B12), molybdenum |

General functions of minerals: (1) **structure** — bones and teeth (Ca, P, Mg, F); (2) parts of **body compounds** — haemoglobin (Fe), thyroxine (I), insulin (Zn), B12 (Co); (3) **fluid and acid–base balance** (Na, K, Cl); (4) **nerve and muscle** excitability (Ca, Na, K, Mg); (5) **enzyme activators** (Mg, Zn, Cu, Mn, Se).

## 3.5 Major minerals

### Calcium

- **Functions**: forms and keeps **bones and teeth** strong (99% of body calcium is in bone); **blood clotting**; **muscle contraction** including the heart; nerve transmission; enzyme activation; cell membrane permeability.
- **Regulation**: vitamin D, parathyroid hormone (raises blood calcium) and calcitonin (lowers it).
- **Absorption** is helped by vitamin D, lactose, protein and an acidic medium; it is reduced by **phytates** (cereal bran), **oxalates** (spinach, amaranth), excess fibre and excess phosphate.
- **Sources**: **milk and milk products** (best source), **ragi** (richest cereal source), green leafy vegetables, sesame (til), small fish eaten with bones, pulses.
- **RDA (2020)**: **1000 mg** per day for adult men and women.
- **Deficiency**: rickets, osteomalacia, **osteoporosis** (especially after menopause), tetany (low blood calcium).

### Phosphorus

- **Functions**: with calcium forms bones and teeth; part of **ATP** (energy), DNA and RNA, phospholipids of cell membranes; phosphate buffer in acid–base balance.
- **Sources**: widely present — milk, meat, fish, egg, cereals, pulses, nuts. Deficiency in normal diets is rare.

### Sodium

- **Functions**: main positive ion of extracellular fluid — controls **fluid volume and blood pressure**, osmotic pressure, acid–base balance, nerve impulses and muscle contraction; helps absorption of glucose and amino acids.
- **Sources**: **common salt** (sodium chloride) is the main source; pickles, papads, sauces, chutneys, chips, processed and bakery foods (baking soda), salted butter, cheese.
- **Intake advice**: the need is small; most Indians eat far more salt than required. WHO advises adults to keep salt below **5 g a day** (about one level teaspoon from all sources). High intake raises blood pressure.
- **Deficiency (hyponatraemia)**: from heavy sweating, vomiting, diarrhoea — cramps, weakness, confusion. Oral rehydration solution replaces it in diarrhoea.

### Potassium

- **Functions**: main positive ion **inside cells**; nerve and **muscle (including heart) function**, fluid balance, acid–base balance; a diet rich in potassium helps lower blood pressure.
- **Sources**: fruits (banana, orange, coconut water, dried fruits), vegetables (potato, tomato, green leafy vegetables), pulses, nuts, meat.
- **Deficiency (hypokalaemia)**: diarrhoea, vomiting, some diuretics — muscle weakness, cramps, irregular heartbeat. **Excess (hyperkalaemia)**: in kidney failure — dangerous heart rhythm problems; such patients limit high-potassium foods (Unit 6).

### Magnesium

- **Functions**: part of bones; activates many enzymes (energy metabolism, ATP); nerve and muscle function; protein synthesis.
- **Sources**: whole grains, pulses, nuts, green leafy vegetables (chlorophyll contains magnesium).
- **RDA (2020)**: man **440 mg**, woman **370 mg**.
- **Deficiency**: in chronic diarrhoea, alcohol use, malabsorption — tremors, muscle twitching, irregular heartbeat, low calcium.

## 3.6 Trace elements

### Iron

- **Functions**: part of **haemoglobin** (oxygen carriage in blood) and **myoglobin** (oxygen store in muscle); enzymes of energy release (cytochromes); immunity and brain development.
- **Forms in food**: **haem iron** (meat, liver, fish, poultry) — well absorbed; **non-haem iron** (cereals, pulses, green leafy vegetables, jaggery, dates) — poorly absorbed.
- **Absorption is increased by**: vitamin C (amla, guava, lemon, tomato eaten with the meal), meat/fish factor, need of the body (pregnancy, deficiency), fermentation and germination of grains and pulses.
- **Absorption is reduced by**: **tea and coffee** (tannins) taken with meals, phytates, oxalates, calcium supplements taken at the same time, antacids, worm infestation causes loss.
- **Sources**: liver, meat, fish, egg; green leafy vegetables (amaranth, drumstick leaves, mint, bathua), **garden cress seeds (halim)**, ragi, bajra, pulses, jaggery, dates, dried fruits; iron-fortified (double fortified) salt and fortified rice.
- **RDA (2020)**: man **19 mg**, woman **29 mg** per day (women lose iron in menstruation). Needs rise in pregnancy.
- **Deficiency**: **iron deficiency anaemia** — the most common nutritional deficiency in India (Unit 5).

### Iodine

- **Functions**: needed to make **thyroid hormones** (thyroxine, T3), which control BMR, growth and brain development.
- **Sources**: **iodised salt** (main source in India), sea fish and seafood; plant foods vary with the soil (low in hilly and flood-prone areas).
- **RDA (2020)**: **150 µg** per day for adult men and women.
- **Deficiency**: iodine deficiency disorders — goitre, hypothyroidism, cretinism, intellectual disability, stillbirths and abortions (Unit 5). **Goitrogens** (cabbage, cauliflower, tapioca in large raw amounts) interfere with iodine use.

### Zinc

- **Functions**: part of over 100 enzymes; growth, wound healing, immunity, taste and smell, insulin storage, sexual maturation.
- **Sources**: meat, fish, egg, milk, whole grains, pulses, nuts.
- **RDA (2020)**: man **17 mg**, woman **13 mg**.
- **Deficiency**: growth retardation, delayed puberty, poor wound healing, loss of taste, diarrhoea; zinc is part of diarrhoea management in children (as per protocol).

### Fluorine (fluoride)

- **Functions**: hardens **tooth enamel** and protects against **dental caries**; helps bone mineralisation.
- **Source**: mainly **drinking water**; tea, sea fish.
- **Problems**: too little → dental caries; **too much (high-fluoride water in parts of India) → fluorosis** — mottled teeth (dental fluorosis) and bone and joint changes (skeletal fluorosis). Defluoridation of water is the prevention.

### Other trace elements (short)

- **Copper**: iron use and haemoglobin formation, enzymes; sources: nuts, liver, whole grains.
- **Selenium**: antioxidant enzyme (glutathione peroxidase), thyroid hormone activation; sources: cereals, seafood, meat.
- **Chromium**: helps insulin action. **Manganese**: enzymes. **Cobalt**: part of vitamin B12.

## 3.7 Summary table of ICMR-NIN 2020 RDA (sedentary adults)

| Nutrient | Man | Woman |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Calcium | 1000 mg | 1000 mg |
| Magnesium | 440 mg | 370 mg |
| Iron | 19 mg | 29 mg |
| Zinc | 17 mg | 13 mg |
| Iodine | 150 µg | 150 µg |
| Thiamine | 1.8 mg | 1.7 mg |
| Riboflavin | 2.5 mg | 2.4 mg |
| Niacin | 18 mg | 14 mg |
| Vitamin B6 | 2.4 mg | 1.9 mg |
| Folate | 300 µg | 220 µg |
| Vitamin B12 | 2.2 µg | 2.2 µg |
| Vitamin C | 80 mg | 65 mg |
| Vitamin A | 1000 µg | 840 µg |
| Vitamin D | 600 IU | 600 IU |

## 3.8 Nursing application

- Advise a **vitamin C source with iron-rich meals** and **no tea or coffee within about an hour of meals** for anaemic patients.
- Encourage **sunlight exposure** of arms and face for vitamin D (elderly, bed-bound, purdah-observing women, indoor workers).
- Teach **use of iodised salt** stored in a closed container away from heat and moisture, added after cooking where possible.
- Promote cheap local sources: ragi for calcium; amaranth, drumstick leaves and garden cress seeds for iron; amla and guava for vitamin C; carrot, papaya and green leafy vegetables for vitamin A.
- Supplements (iron, folic acid, vitamin A, vitamin D, calcium) are given only as prescribed or as per national programme protocols, because some can be harmful in excess.
- Watch potassium and sodium in kidney, heart and liver patients (Unit 6).

## Remember

- Fat-soluble: A, D, E, K (stored, can be toxic); water-soluble: B complex and C (not stored, lost in cooking).
- Vitamin A → rhodopsin, night vision; carotene in green leafy and yellow vegetables; RDA man 1000 µg, woman 840 µg.
- Vitamin D from sunlight; calcium absorption; rickets/osteomalacia; RDA 600 IU.
- Vitamin K → clotting factors; newborn bleeding.
- B1 beriberi; B2 angular stomatitis; niacin pellagra (3 D's); folate and B12 megaloblastic anaemia; C scurvy.
- B12 only in animal foods; amla richest common vitamin C source.
- Major minerals: Ca, P, Na, K, Mg; trace: Fe, I, Zn, Cu, F, Se.
- Calcium RDA 1000 mg; best sources milk and ragi; phytates and oxalates reduce absorption.
- Iron RDA man 19 mg, woman 29 mg; vitamin C helps, tea and coffee hinder.
- Iodine 150 µg; iodised salt; goitre, cretinism. Fluoride: too little caries, too much fluorosis.
- Salt: keep below 5 g a day (WHO).

# Unit 4: Balanced diet and nutrition across the life cycle

INC Unit VII (7 hours theory + 8 hours lab) — the largest unit of the course. Two parts: **balanced diet** (definition, principles, steps, food guides, RDA, food exchange system, calculating nutritive value, dietary fibre) and **nutrition across the life cycle** (meal planning, IYCF, diets for children, adolescents, elderly, pregnancy, anaemia in pregnancy and lactation). The lab sessions — preparing balanced diets and low-cost nutritious dishes — are based on this unit.

## 4.1 Balanced diet

**Definition.** A balanced diet contains a **variety of foods in such quantities and proportions** that the need for energy, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals and other nutrients is fully met, with a **small margin of extra nutrients** to cover short periods of low intake.

### Principles of a balanced diet

1. **Adequacy** — meets the RDA/EAR of the person for energy and all nutrients.
2. **Balance** — right proportion among nutrients (e.g. not all energy from cereals; protein, fat and carbohydrate in reasonable shares).
3. **Variety** — foods from every food group every day; different vegetables and fruits through the week.
4. **Moderation** — limit salt, sugar, fried foods, refined foods and alcohol.
5. **Calorie control** — energy in = energy out for healthy weight.
6. **Nutrient density** — choose foods that give many nutrients per calorie (vegetables, pulses, milk) over "empty calories" (sugar, soft drinks).
7. **Individualisation** — suits age, sex, activity, physiological state, health, budget, culture, religion, likes and local availability.
8. **Safety** — clean, safe food and water.

### Steps in planning a balanced diet

1. Find the person's **age, sex, body weight, activity level and physiological state** (pregnant, lactating, ill).
2. Look up the **requirements** (ICMR-NIN 2020 RDA/EAR) for energy, protein and key nutrients.
3. Decide the **number of portions** from each food group (cereals, pulses, milk, vegetables, fruits, fats and sugar) using the food guide or exchange lists.
4. **Distribute** the foods across meals — breakfast, mid-morning, lunch, evening, dinner (and bedtime milk if needed).
5. **Select dishes** suited to the family's habits, budget and season.
6. **Calculate** the nutritive value of the planned day's diet and compare with the requirement; adjust.
7. Check variety, colour, texture, taste and cost.

## 4.2 Food guides — Basic Four Food Groups

A **food guide** groups foods with similar nutrients so a person can choose a balanced diet without calculations.

| Group | Foods | Main nutrients | Daily advice (simple) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **1. Cereals, millets and their products** (with roots and tubers) | Rice, wheat, ragi, jowar, bajra, maize, oats, potato | Energy, carbohydrate, some protein, B vitamins, fibre (whole grains) | Main part of every meal; prefer whole grains and millets |
| **2. Protein foods** — pulses, legumes, milk, egg, meat, fish, nuts | Dal, rajma, chana, soy, milk, curd, paneer, egg, chicken, fish, groundnut | Protein, calcium (milk), iron, B12 (animal foods) | Pulses or animal foods at two meals; milk or curd daily |
| **3. Vegetables and fruits** | Green leafy vegetables, other vegetables, roots, seasonal fruits | Vitamins (A, C, folate), minerals, fibre | Several servings daily including a green leafy vegetable and a fruit |
| **4. Fats, oils and sugar** | Oils, ghee, butter, sugar, jaggery | Energy, essential fatty acids (oils) | In small amounts only |

The newer ICMR-NIN guidance ("My Plate for the Day") makes the same point with a plate: about half the plate as vegetables and fruits, the rest shared by cereals and millets, pulses/meat/egg, milk or curd, and a small amount of nuts and seeds, with limited oil, salt and sugar. Check the current ICMR-NIN Dietary Guidelines for Indians for the exact daily amounts.

```text
     A SIMPLE BALANCED PLATE (lunch)
 ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐
 │  Vegetables & greens  │  Cereal /    │
 │  (half the plate with │  millet      │
 │   salad and fruit)    │  (roti/rice) │
 │                       ├──────────────┤
 │                       │ Dal / egg /  │
 │                       │ fish / paneer│
 └──────────────────────────────────────┘
       + a bowl of curd or glass of milk
       + a little oil, salt and sugar only
```

## 4.3 RDA — definition, uses and limitations

**Definition.** The **Recommended Dietary Allowance** is the average daily intake of a nutrient that is sufficient to meet the requirement of nearly all (about 97–98%) healthy individuals of a particular age, sex and physiological group. ICMR-NIN 2020 also gives the **EAR** (meets the need of half the group) and **tolerable upper limits**.

**Uses of RDA**

- Planning diets for individuals, families and institutions (hostels, hospitals, prisons, the army).
- Planning food supply, food production and national nutrition policy.
- Planning supplementary feeding programmes (ICDS, PM POSHAN).
- Evaluating diet surveys — judging whether a population eats enough (ICMR-NIN 2020 advises using the EAR for this).
- Food labelling and fortification standards.
- Nutrition education.

**Limitations of RDA**

- Meant for **healthy** people — not for the sick, who need therapeutic diets.
- Based on **reference body weights** (65 kg man, 55 kg woman); must be adjusted for actual weight and activity.
- **Not an individual's exact requirement** — the RDA is above most people's need, so eating less than the RDA does not mean deficiency.
- Do not cover all nutrients; values change as research advances (2010 and 2020 values differ).
- Do not account for nutrient losses in cooking and differences in bioavailability in every food.
- Does not consider food habits, cost or taste.

### ICMR-NIN 2020 energy and protein for children and adolescents (RDA)

| Age group | Reference weight (kg) | Energy (kcal/day) | Protein (g/day) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1–3 years | 12.9 | 1110 | 12.5 |
| 4–6 years | 18.3 | 1360 | 15.9 |
| 7–9 years | 25.3 | 1700 | 23.3 |
| Boys 10–12 years | 34.9 | 2220 | 31.8 |
| Girls 10–12 years | 36.4 | 2060 | 32.8 |
| Boys 13–15 years | 50.5 | 2860 | 44.9 |
| Girls 13–15 years | 49.6 | 2400 | 43.2 |
| Boys 16–18 years | 64.4 | 3320 | 55.4 |
| Girls 16–18 years | 55.7 | 2500 | 46.2 |

(The 2020 summary table lists 1070 kcal for 1–3 years while the detailed table gives 1110; learn "about 1100 kcal".) Adult values are in Unit 2.

## 4.4 Food exchange system

**Definition.** Foods are grouped into lists so that one portion ("exchange") of any food in a list gives **about the same energy, carbohydrate, protein and fat** as any other in that list. Foods within a list can then be swapped without upsetting the diet plan.

**Uses**: diabetic and weight-reduction diets, renal diets, giving variety and choice to patients, simple counting of calories without tables.

Approximate exchange values commonly used in Indian dietary guidance (use the hospital's own list in practice):

| Exchange list | One portion | Approx. energy | Approx. protein |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Cereals and millets | 30 g raw (e.g. 1 medium roti or ½ cup cooked rice) | 100 kcal | 3 g |
| Pulses and legumes | 30 g raw (1 small bowl dal) | 100 kcal | 6 g |
| Milk (toned) | 100 ml | 70 kcal | 3 g |
| Vegetables | 100 g | about 30 kcal | small |
| Fruits | 100 g | about 40 kcal | small |
| Fats and oils | 5 g (1 teaspoon) | 45 kcal | 0 |
| Sugar | 5 g (1 teaspoon) | 20 kcal | 0 |

Example swaps: 1 roti ↔ ½ cup cooked rice ↔ about 2 small idlis; 1 bowl dal ↔ 1 egg ↔ about 30 g paneer (roughly similar protein).

## 4.5 Calculation of the nutritive value of foods

**Tool**: the **Indian Food Composition Tables (IFCT)** published by ICMR-NIN give nutrients per 100 g edible portion.

**Steps**

1. List every food eaten in the day and its **raw weight** (edible portion).
2. Find the nutrient content **per 100 g** of each food from the food composition table.
3. Calculate: **nutrient in the food = (nutrient per 100 g × weight eaten) ÷ 100**.
4. Add the values for all foods to get the day's total.
5. Compare with the RDA/EAR; work out the percentage met; adjust the diet.

**Worked example (using the exchange values above):**

| Food (raw) | Amount | Energy (kcal) | Protein (g) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Cereals | 240 g = 8 exchanges | 800 | 24 |
| Pulses | 60 g = 2 exchanges | 200 | 12 |
| Milk (toned) | 400 ml | 280 | 12 |
| Vegetables | 300 g | 90 | — |
| Fruit | 100 g | 40 | — |
| Oil | 20 g | 180 | 0 |
| Sugar | 15 g | 60 | 0 |
| **Total** | | **1650** | **48** |

This meets the energy (1660 kcal) and protein (45.7 g) RDA of a sedentary woman. Vegetable and fruit protein is small and left out for simplicity.

## 4.6 Dietary fibre

**Definition.** The parts of plant foods that human digestive enzymes cannot digest (non-starch polysaccharides and lignin).

| Insoluble fibre | Soluble fibre |
| --- | --- |
| Cellulose, hemicellulose, lignin | Pectin, gums, mucilage, beta-glucan |
| Whole wheat, bran, whole grains, vegetables, skins of fruits | Fruits (apple, guava), oats, barley, pulses, fenugreek seeds, isabgol |
| Adds bulk, speeds passage through the gut, prevents constipation | Forms a gel; slows glucose absorption; binds bile acids and lowers cholesterol |

**Benefits**: prevents constipation, piles and diverticular disease; improves blood glucose control; lowers cholesterol; gives fullness and helps weight control; feeds healthy gut bacteria; linked with lower risk of colon cancer.

**Excess**: gas and bloating, reduced absorption of iron, zinc and calcium (phytates). Fibre should be increased slowly with plenty of water. (ICMR-NIN gives a fibre recommendation linked to energy intake — check the current guideline for the figure.)

## 4.7 Meal planning (menu planning)

**Definition.** Planning the meals for a day or a week for a person or family so that nutritional needs are met in an acceptable, affordable and practical way.

**Principles**: meet nutritional needs; suit the family's budget, habits and culture; use seasonal and local foods; give variety in colour, texture, flavour and cooking method; save time, fuel and effort; reduce nutrient loss; consider the needs of special members (child, pregnant woman, elderly, patient); spread food across the day.

**Steps**: (1) find family members' needs; (2) decide the meal pattern (number of meals); (3) choose the main dish and then the side dishes from each food group; (4) plan the market list and budget; (5) check the plan against the food guide; (6) evaluate acceptance and adjust.

**Low-cost nutritious ideas** (lab): khichdi with vegetables, sprouted moong or chana chaat, ragi porridge or ragi roti, vegetable upma or poha with peanuts, dal-palak, besan chilla, sattu drink, groundnut-jaggery laddoo, mixed vegetable paratha, curd rice with vegetables. Germination, fermentation and combining cereals with pulses improve value at little cost.

## 4.8 Infant and Young Child Feeding (IYCF)

India's national IYCF guidance (MoHFW/MWCD, in line with WHO and UNICEF) recommends:

1. **Early initiation of breastfeeding within one hour of birth** — give colostrum; no prelacteal feeds (honey, sugar water, ghutti).
2. **Exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months** — no water, other milk, or foods (prescribed medicines and ORS allowed).
3. **Timely complementary feeding from six months** (completed 180 days), adequate in amount, frequency, consistency and variety, while continuing breastfeeding.
4. **Continued breastfeeding till two years of age or beyond.**
5. **Responsive feeding** and **safe, hygienic** preparation.
6. **Feeding during and after illness** — continue breastfeeding and food during illness; give extra food after recovery.
7. Special support for low birth weight babies and for feeding in difficult situations.

### Breastfeeding

**Advantages for the baby**: perfect nutrition, easily digested; colostrum rich in antibodies and vitamin A ("first immunisation"); protects against diarrhoea, pneumonia and ear infections; lower risk of obesity and diabetes later; better brain development; bonding. **For the mother**: helps the uterus contract, reduces postpartum bleeding, helps spacing of births (lactational amenorrhoea), lowers the risk of breast and ovarian cancer, saves money. **For the family and nation**: no cost, always available, safe and at the right temperature.

**Nurse's role**: help the mother start within an hour; teach correct **position and attachment** (baby's chin touching the breast, mouth wide open, lower lip turned out, more areola visible above than below); feed on demand, 8 or more times in 24 hours; signs of enough milk (6 or more wet nappies a day, steady weight gain); express and store milk for working mothers; manage sore nipples and engorgement; discourage bottles.

### Infant foods and complementary feeding (weaning)

**Complementary feeding** means giving other foods along with breast milk from six months, when breast milk alone cannot meet the baby's needs for energy, iron and other nutrients.

**Principles**: start at six months; start with small amounts of soft, mashed food and increase slowly; one new food at a time; thick consistency (food should stay on the spoon), not watery; energy-dense — add a little oil or ghee; feed from a clean bowl and spoon, not a bottle; respond to hunger cues; continue breastfeeding.

**Suggested progression (as in national IYCF guidance)**

| Age | Texture and examples | Frequency (besides breast milk) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 6–8 months | Mashed, semi-solid: thick dal-rice, mashed khichdi, suji or ragi porridge with milk, mashed banana, potato | 2–3 meals a day |
| 9–11 months | Finely chopped / mashed family foods, finger foods: soft idli, chopped vegetables, egg | 3–4 meals + snacks |
| 12–24 months | Family foods, cut small | 3–4 meals + 1–2 snacks |

Home-made infant foods can be made cheaply from roasted cereal + pulse flour mixtures (e.g. wheat, ragi or rice with roasted chana or moong) with jaggery and a little oil. ICDS provides take-home ration for children 6 months to 3 years.

## 4.9 Diets for children, adolescents and the elderly

### Pre-school and school children (1–12 years)

- Rapid growth and high activity — high needs for energy, protein, calcium, iron and vitamin A relative to body size; small stomachs → **small frequent meals** (3 meals + 2 snacks).
- Include milk (calcium), pulses or egg (protein), green leafy vegetables and fruits (iron, vitamins A and C).
- Avoid junk food, sugary drinks and too much tea; establish breakfast; hand washing before meals; regular deworming as per programme.
- School children: packed lunch with cereal-pulse dish plus vegetable; PM POSHAN hot cooked meal.
- Problems: under-nutrition, anaemia, dental caries, and increasingly obesity.

### Adolescents (10–19 years)

- **Growth spurt** — energy and protein needs reach their highest (see table); **calcium** for peak bone mass; **iron** — girls lose iron in menstruation, boys gain muscle and blood volume.
- Adolescent girls need good nutrition to prepare for safe motherhood (anaemia in a girl → anaemia in pregnancy → low birth weight baby — the intergenerational cycle).
- Problems: skipping breakfast, fast food, dieting to lose weight, eating disorders, anaemia, obesity.
- Advice: three meals and healthy snacks; milk and milk products; pulses, egg, meat; green leafy vegetables and fruits; limit fried foods and sugary drinks; weekly iron-folic acid under WIFS/AMB (Unit 8).

### Elderly (60 years and above)

- **Energy need falls** (lower BMR and activity), but **protein, calcium, vitamin D, B12 and fibre needs stay the same or rise**.
- Problems: poor teeth or dentures, less taste and smell, less saliva, poor appetite, constipation, less thirst (dehydration), loneliness and depression, chronic diseases and many medicines, low income.
- Diet plan: **soft, easily chewed, easily digested** food; small frequent meals; enough protein (milk, curd, dal, egg, paneer); calcium and vitamin D (milk, ragi, sunlight); fibre and **plenty of fluids** (constipation); less salt, sugar and fat; avoid heavy fried meals at night.

## 4.10 Diet in pregnancy

### Why needs increase

Growth of the foetus, placenta, uterus and breasts; increase in the mother's blood volume and red cells; fat store for lactation; higher BMR.

### Nutritional requirements (ICMR-NIN 2020)

- **Energy**: **+ 350 kcal/day** over her normal need (second and third trimesters), adjusted for weight gain and activity.
- **Protein**: **+ 9.5 g/day in the 2nd trimester, + 22 g/day in the 3rd trimester** (RDA).
- Higher needs for **iron, folic acid, calcium, iodine, vitamin B12, vitamin A, vitamin C and zinc** (see the full ICMR-NIN 2020 report for the exact pregnancy values).

### Balanced diet plan for a pregnant woman (sample day, household measures)

| Time | Food |
| --- | --- |
| Early morning | 1 glass milk; a few soaked almonds or roasted chana |
| Breakfast | 2 vegetable-stuffed parathas or 2–3 idlis with sambar; 1 boiled egg (if eaten) |
| Mid-morning | 1 seasonal fruit (guava, orange or banana) |
| Lunch | 2–3 rotis or rice, 1 bowl dal, 1 bowl green leafy vegetable (palak, methi), salad, 1 bowl curd |
| Evening | Sprouted moong chaat or ragi laddoo; buttermilk or lemon water |
| Dinner | Rice or roti, dal or rajma or fish/chicken, mixed vegetable, salad |
| Bedtime | 1 glass milk |

**Key advice**: eat one extra small meal a day; include milk and curd, pulses, green leafy vegetables and fruit daily; use **iodised salt**; take the iron-folic acid tablets and calcium given at the antenatal clinic as advised; avoid alcohol and tobacco; limit tea and coffee; avoid unpasteurised milk and undercooked meat; small frequent meals for nausea and heartburn; fibre and water for constipation; no food taboos that cut out nutritious foods. Gain weight steadily as advised by the antenatal team.

## 4.11 Anaemia in pregnancy

**Diagnosis**: WHO defines anaemia in pregnancy as **haemoglobin below 11 g/dL**. Severity: mild 10–10.9, moderate 7–9.9, severe below 7 g/dL. Signs: pallor of conjunctiva, tongue, palms and nails; tiredness; breathlessness; palpitations; swelling of feet; spoon-shaped nails (koilonychia) in long-standing iron deficiency. Hb is checked at the first antenatal visit and repeated during pregnancy.

**Causes**: low iron, folate and B12 intake; increased need; repeated pregnancies with short gaps; worm infestation; malaria; blood loss; poor absorption (tea with meals).

**Risks**: preterm birth, low birth weight, maternal fatigue, heart failure in severe anaemia, poor tolerance of bleeding at delivery and higher maternal death.

**Diet for an anaemic pregnant woman**: iron-rich foods at every meal — green leafy vegetables (amaranth, drumstick leaves, bathua, mint), garden cress seeds (halim), ragi, bajra, pulses and sprouts, jaggery, dates, dried fruits; meat, liver, fish, egg if eaten; **a vitamin C source with each meal** (amla, guava, lemon, orange, tomato); cook in iron vessels; **avoid tea and coffee with meals**; folate-rich foods; protein-rich foods.

**Iron and folic acid supplementation**: under the **Anemia Mukt Bharat** programme, every pregnant woman receives prophylactic iron-folic acid tablets daily from the second trimester for about 180 days and also after delivery, and is treated for anaemia when detected, as per the national protocol. Deworming is given once in the second trimester as per protocol. (Doses are set by the national guideline — follow it; do not memorise from unofficial sources.)

**Counselling points for IFA**: take the tablet after food or at bedtime to reduce nausea; take it with water or lemon water, **not with tea, coffee or milk**; keep calcium tablets at a different time; stools may turn black — this is harmless; mild constipation can be eased with fibre and water; complete the full course even if feeling well; keep tablets away from children (iron overdose is dangerous for children); report severe side effects.

## 4.12 Nutrition in lactation

**Requirements (ICMR-NIN 2020)**: energy **+ 600 kcal/day (0–6 months)** and **+ 520 kcal/day (7–12 months)**; protein **+ 16.9 g/day (0–6 months)** and **+ 13.2 g/day (6–12 months)** over her normal need. Needs for calcium, iron (to replace stores), vitamin A, B vitamins, vitamin C, iodine and **fluids** are also higher.

**Diet for a lactating mother**: one extra meal plus an extra snack a day; **plenty of fluids** — water, milk, buttermilk, soups, dal water (drink a glass of water or milk at each feed); milk and milk products; pulses, egg, fish, meat; green leafy vegetables and fruits; traditional galactagogue foods (methi, garlic, dill, sesame, dry fruit laddoos) are acceptable if balanced; avoid alcohol and smoking; continue iron-folic acid and calcium as advised after delivery; avoid restricting foods because of taboos (e.g. not giving vegetables or water after delivery).

**Complementary feeding / weaning** is covered under IYCF (4.8): start at 6 months, continue breastfeeding to two years or beyond.

## 4.13 Nursing application

- Plan diets with the family's own foods and budget; use household measures (katori, glass, teaspoon) rather than grams.
- Teach "eat a rainbow": something from every food group every day.
- Weigh children monthly (growth chart) and pregnant women at every visit.
- Promote breastfeeding from the first hour; support working mothers.
- Counsel on IFA tablets and iron-rich diet; check Hb as per schedule.
- Elderly: check teeth, appetite, fluid intake and loneliness.

## Remember

- Balanced diet = variety of foods meeting all nutrient needs with a small safety margin.
- Basic four food groups: cereals; protein foods; vegetables and fruits; fats, oils, sugar.
- RDA covers nearly all healthy people; meant for healthy groups, not exact individual need; EAR for assessing groups.
- Food exchange = foods in a list interchangeable for energy and macronutrients; used in diabetic diets.
- Nutritive value = (nutrient per 100 g × amount) ÷ 100, from IFCT.
- Soluble fibre lowers glucose and cholesterol; insoluble prevents constipation.
- IYCF: breastfeed within 1 hour, exclusive 6 months, complementary from 6 months, continue 2 years and beyond.
- Pregnancy: +350 kcal; protein +9.5 g (2nd) and +22 g (3rd trimester); anaemia = Hb below 11 g/dL.
- Lactation: +600 kcal (0–6 months), +520 kcal (7–12 months); protein +16.9 g then +13.2 g; plenty of fluids.
- Elderly: fewer calories, same protein, soft food, more fluid and fibre.

# Unit 5: Nutritional deficiency disorders

INC Unit VIII (6 hours): protein energy malnutrition (PEM) including severe acute malnutrition (SAM), childhood obesity, vitamin A, B, C and D deficiency disorders, and iron, iodine and calcium deficiencies — for each the causes, signs and symptoms, management, prevention and the nurse's role. This unit is a favourite for essay questions; learn one complete answer for PEM and one for vitamin A deficiency.

## 5.1 Protein energy malnutrition (PEM)

**Definition.** A range of conditions that arise from a lack of protein and energy in varying proportions, most common in children under five, and usually worsened by infections. WHO now prefers the term **undernutrition** and measures it as stunting, wasting and underweight.

### Magnitude of the problem

- Undernutrition is a major underlying cause of child deaths in India and a cause of poor growth and learning.
- **NFHS-5 (2019–21), children under five**: **35.5% stunted** (low height-for-age), **19.3% wasted** (low weight-for-height), **32.1% underweight** (low weight-for-age); **67.1%** of children aged 6–59 months were anaemic. Check the latest National Family Health Survey fact sheet for newer figures.
- It is highest in poor, rural and tribal families, in low birth weight babies, and in the 6–24 month age group when complementary feeding begins.

### Causes

| Group | Causes |
| --- | --- |
| **Immediate** | Inadequate food intake (amount, frequency, quality); repeated **infections** — diarrhoea, measles, respiratory infections, worms |
| **Underlying** | Household food insecurity; poor IYCF practices — late initiation of breastfeeding, early or late complementary feeding, watery diluted feeds, bottle feeding; poor maternal nutrition and low birth weight; poor water, sanitation and hygiene; poor access to health care |
| **Basic** | Poverty, illiteracy (especially of the mother), large family, closely spaced births, low status of women, food taboos, social inequality, disasters |

### Classification

**1. Clinical (Wellcome Trust classification)** — uses weight-for-age as % of the standard and the presence of oedema:

| Weight-for-age (% of standard) | Oedema present | Oedema absent |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 60–80% | **Kwashiorkor** | Underweight |
| Below 60% | **Marasmic kwashiorkor** | **Marasmus** |

**2. Indian Academy of Paediatrics (IAP) classification** (weight-for-age, % of standard): normal above 80%; grade I 71–80%; grade II 61–70%; grade III 51–60%; grade IV 50% or less. A letter "K" is added if oedema is present.

**3. WHO classification (current, used in programmes)** — compares the child with the WHO Child Growth Standards using Z-scores (standard deviation units):

| Indicator | What it shows | Moderate | Severe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Weight-for-height (wasting)** | Acute malnutrition | −3 to < −2 SD | < −3 SD |
| **Height-for-age (stunting)** | Chronic malnutrition | −3 to < −2 SD | < −3 SD |
| **Weight-for-age (underweight)** | Composite | −3 to < −2 SD | < −3 SD |

### Marasmus and kwashiorkor compared

| Feature | Marasmus | Kwashiorkor |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Main deficiency | Energy (and protein) — "starvation" | Mainly protein, often with infection; energy relatively less short |
| Age | Usually under 1 year | Usually 1–3 years (after weaning) |
| Oedema | **Absent** | **Present** (pitting, feet and legs, may be general) |
| Weight | Very low (below 60%) | 60–80% (oedema hides the loss) |
| Muscle wasting | Severe — "skin and bones", old-man face | Present but masked by oedema |
| Subcutaneous fat | Absent | Present (reduced) |
| Face | Wrinkled, monkey-like | Moon face |
| Mental state | Alert, hungry | Apathetic, irritable, miserable |
| Appetite | Good | Poor |
| Hair | Usually normal or thin | Thin, sparse, easily pluckable, lighter colour ("flag sign" of alternating bands) |
| Skin | Dry, loose folds | **Flaky paint dermatosis**, ulcers |
| Liver | Not enlarged | **Enlarged (fatty liver)** |
| Serum albumin | Normal or slightly low | Very low |
| Prognosis | Better with feeding | Higher risk of death |

### Severe acute malnutrition (SAM)

In children aged **6–59 months**, SAM is diagnosed by **any one** of:

- **Weight-for-height (or length) below −3 SD** of the WHO standards, or
- **Mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC) below 11.5 cm**, or
- **Bilateral pitting oedema** of nutritional origin.

**Moderate acute malnutrition (MAM)**: weight-for-height −3 to < −2 SD, or MUAC 11.5 to < 12.5 cm.

**MUAC tape colours** used by health workers: red (below 11.5 cm) = SAM; yellow (11.5–12.5 cm) = MAM; green (12.5 cm and above) = normal.

```text
SCREENING A CHILD 6–59 MONTHS
 Bilateral pitting oedema? ──yes──► SAM
        │ no
 MUAC < 11.5 cm or WFH < −3 SD? ──yes──► SAM
        │ no
 MUAC 11.5–12.4 cm or WFH −3 to −2 SD? ──yes──► MAM
        │ no
 Normal → continue growth monitoring
 SAM + medical complication or failed appetite test → admit to NRC
 SAM, no complication, good appetite → community-based care
```

**Signs and symptoms of PEM** (general): growth failure and weight loss; muscle wasting; loss of fat under skin; oedema (kwashiorkor); hair and skin changes; apathy or irritability; anaemia; signs of vitamin deficiencies (Bitot's spots, angular stomatitis); diarrhoea and infections; hypothermia and hypoglycaemia in severe cases.

### Management of SAM

**Where**: children with SAM and **medical complications** (or no appetite, or oedema of all limbs) are admitted to a **Nutrition Rehabilitation Centre (NRC)** or hospital; uncomplicated cases with good appetite can be managed in the community (community-based management of acute malnutrition) as per state protocol.

**Facility management follows the WHO "ten steps"**, in two phases — **stabilisation** (first few days) and **rehabilitation**:

1. Treat or prevent **hypoglycaemia** — feed early and frequently, day and night.
2. Treat or prevent **hypothermia** — keep warm (kangaroo care, covered head, warm room), feed often.
3. Treat or prevent **dehydration** — with the special low-sodium rehydration solution for malnourished children (ReSoMal), given slowly; avoid fast IV fluids, which can cause heart failure.
4. Correct **electrolyte imbalance** — these children have low potassium and magnesium and excess body sodium.
5. Treat or prevent **infection** — antibiotics as per protocol, since signs of infection are often hidden.
6. Correct **micronutrient deficiencies** — vitamin A, folic acid, zinc, copper; **iron is started only in the rehabilitation phase**, once the child is gaining weight.
7. **Start cautious feeding** — small frequent feeds of starter therapeutic milk (F-75) in the stabilisation phase.
8. Achieve **catch-up growth** — catch-up formula (F-100) or ready-to-use therapeutic food in rehabilitation; aim for rapid weight gain.
9. Provide **sensory stimulation and emotional support** — play, loving care.
10. Prepare for **follow-up** after recovery — teach the mother to feed with home foods, immunise, follow up at the NRC/anganwadi.

Discharge and follow-up criteria are given in the national/state SAM guidelines.

### Prevention of PEM

- **Maternal nutrition** and care in pregnancy to prevent low birth weight.
- **Breastfeeding** within one hour, exclusive for 6 months, continued to 2 years; timely, adequate complementary feeding.
- **Growth monitoring** every month (Mother and Child Protection card) to catch growth faltering early.
- **Supplementary nutrition** through ICDS anganwadis (take-home ration, hot cooked meals), PM POSHAN in schools.
- **Immunisation** (measles), **deworming**, ORS and zinc for diarrhoea, early treatment of infections.
- Safe water, sanitation, hand washing.
- Family planning and birth spacing; women's education and empowerment.
- Nutrition education using low-cost local foods.

### Nurse's role in PEM

- **Assessment**: weigh and measure, plot on the growth chart, measure MUAC, check for bilateral pitting oedema (press both feet for 3 seconds), look for danger signs and vitamin deficiencies.
- **Referral**: SAM with complications to NRC; follow-up of discharged children.
- **Care in NRC/ward**: feeding by the clock including at night, keeping warm, monitoring weight daily, temperature, pulse, respiration, signs of over-hydration; infection control; play and stimulation; recording intake.
- **Education**: teach the mother preparation of energy-dense home foods, feeding frequency, hygiene, continued feeding in illness.
- **Community**: work with ASHA and anganwadi worker in screening, home visits and counselling.

## 5.2 Childhood obesity

**Definition**: excess body fat that harms health. In children it is judged with **WHO growth standards**: for under-five children, weight-for-height above +2 SD = overweight and above +3 SD = obese; for 5–19 years, **BMI-for-age above +1 SD = overweight and above +2 SD = obesity**.

**Causes**: energy-dense junk food and sugary drinks; large portions; low physical activity, long screen time; poor sleep; family history and parental obesity; using food as a reward; less breastfeeding; rarely, hormonal (hypothyroidism) or genetic causes or drugs.

**Signs and symptoms**: excess weight, fat around the abdomen, stretch marks, dark velvety skin in neck folds (acanthosis nigricans — a sign of insulin resistance), breathlessness on exertion, snoring and sleep apnoea, knee pain, early puberty in girls, low self-esteem and bullying.

**Assessment**: weight, height, BMI-for-age plotted on growth charts, waist circumference, diet and activity history, blood pressure, and blood sugar and lipids as advised.

**Complications**: type 2 diabetes, hypertension, high cholesterol, fatty liver, orthopaedic problems, polycystic ovary syndrome, depression; obesity in childhood tends to continue into adult life.

**Management and prevention**: involve the whole family; no crash diets — aim to slow weight gain while the child grows; regular meals with breakfast; more vegetables, fruits, whole grains and pulses; water and milk instead of sugary drinks; fewer fried and packaged snacks; at least an hour of active play a day; limit screen time; enough sleep; healthy school canteens; positive praise, not shaming.

**Nurse's role**: screening in schools and clinics, plotting BMI-for-age, counselling the family, school health education, encouraging sports, referral for complications.

## 5.3 Vitamin A deficiency (VAD)

**Causes**: low intake of vitamin A and carotene-rich foods; poor fat intake; malabsorption; repeated infections (diarrhoea, measles) that use up stores; PEM; worm infestation; lack of breastfeeding.

**Signs — WHO classification of xerophthalmia**:

| Code | Sign |
| --- | --- |
| XN | **Night blindness** — earliest symptom; child cannot see in dim light |
| X1A | Conjunctival xerosis — dry, wrinkled, dull conjunctiva |
| X1B | **Bitot's spots** — foamy, cheesy, triangular white spots on the conjunctiva, usually lateral |
| X2 | Corneal xerosis — dry, hazy cornea |
| X3A | Corneal ulceration/keratomalacia covering less than one third of the cornea |
| X3B | Keratomalacia covering one third or more — the cornea softens and melts; permanent blindness |
| XS | Corneal scar |
| XF | Xerophthalmic fundus — white spots on the retina |

Other signs: dry rough skin (follicular hyperkeratosis), poor growth, frequent infections and higher deaths from measles and diarrhoea.

**Management**: high-dose vitamin A given as per the national treatment schedule on diagnosis (doctor's order); treat infections and PEM; eye care with antibiotic eye drops as ordered; protect the eye; vitamin A-rich diet.

**Prevention**: (1) **Short term** — periodic vitamin A supplementation for children 9 months to 5 years under the national programme (Unit 8); (2) **Medium term** — food fortification (vitamin A-fortified oil and milk); (3) **Long term** — diet: green leafy vegetables, yellow-orange fruits and vegetables, milk, egg, liver, cooked with a little oil; breastfeeding (colostrum); measles immunisation; deworming; kitchen gardens.

**Nurse's role**: screen children's eyes for Bitot's spots and ask about night blindness; give vitamin A as per the programme schedule and record it; educate mothers on cheap carotene sources; refer corneal cases urgently.

## 5.4 Vitamin B deficiency disorders

| Disorder | Cause | Signs and symptoms | Management and prevention |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Beriberi (B1, thiamine)** | Diet of highly polished rice; washing rice repeatedly; alcoholism | **Dry beriberi**: peripheral neuritis — tingling, numbness, calf tenderness, foot drop, difficulty getting up from squatting. **Wet beriberi**: oedema, breathlessness, palpitations, heart failure. **Infantile beriberi** in breastfed babies of deficient mothers. **Wernicke–Korsakoff** syndrome in alcoholics | Thiamine as prescribed; parboiled or unpolished rice, whole grains, pulses, nuts; don't wash rice too much or discard cooking water; reduce alcohol |
| **Riboflavin (B2) deficiency** (ariboflavinosis) | Low milk and green vegetable intake | **Angular stomatitis** (cracks at the mouth corners), **cheilosis**, **glossitis** (magenta, sore tongue), scaly skin around nose, eye watering and burning | B-complex as prescribed; milk, curd, green leafy vegetables, egg, pulses |
| **Pellagra (niacin)** | Maize- or jowar-based diet (jowar has excess leucine which interferes with niacin), alcoholism | **Dermatitis** (dark rough skin on sun-exposed parts — "Casal's necklace" on the neck), **diarrhoea**, **dementia** — and death if untreated (4 D's) | Niacin as prescribed; groundnut, pulses, meat, fish, milk; varied cereals |
| **Pyridoxine (B6) deficiency** | Long isoniazid treatment, alcoholism | Peripheral neuritis, convulsions in infants, anaemia, glossitis | Pyridoxine as prescribed alongside isoniazid as per protocol; varied diet |
| **Folate deficiency** | Low green vegetable intake, pregnancy, overcooking, some drugs, alcohol | **Megaloblastic anaemia**, glossitis; in pregnancy — **neural tube defects** in the baby | Folate-rich food; IFA supplementation as per programme; periconceptional folic acid as advised |
| **Vitamin B12 deficiency** | Strict vegetarian (vegan) diet, lack of intrinsic factor (pernicious anaemia), gastric surgery, tapeworm, elderly | **Megaloblastic anaemia**, sore tongue, numbness and tingling, loss of position sense, memory loss; nerve damage can be permanent | B12 as prescribed (injections when absorption fails); milk, curd, egg, meat, fish |

## 5.5 Vitamin C deficiency — scurvy

**Causes**: diets lacking fresh fruits and vegetables; overcooking and long storage; infants fed only boiled animal milk without fruit; elderly living alone; alcoholism.

**Signs and symptoms**: fatigue and weakness; **swollen, spongy, bleeding gums**; loose teeth; small bleeds around hair follicles (perifollicular haemorrhages) and bruising; **poor wound healing** and reopening of old wounds; joint and bone pain; anaemia. In infants (infantile scurvy): painful swollen legs, the baby lies with legs flexed and cries when touched ("pseudoparalysis"), bleeding gums once teeth erupt.

**Management**: vitamin C as prescribed; daily fresh fruits and vegetables — amla, guava, orange, lemon, tomato, sprouts; gentle handling of painful limbs; oral hygiene.

**Prevention**: fresh fruit daily; eat vegetables raw (salads) or lightly cooked; cut vegetables just before cooking; sprouting pulses; avoid soda in cooking.

## 5.6 Vitamin D deficiency — rickets and osteomalacia

**Causes**: little sunlight exposure (indoor life, covered clothing, pollution, dark skin, swaddled babies); low dietary vitamin D and calcium; malabsorption; liver or kidney disease; prolonged exclusive breastfeeding of babies of deficient mothers without sun exposure.

**Rickets (children)**: delayed closure of the anterior fontanelle, soft skull bones (craniotabes), **frontal bossing**; **rickety rosary** (beading at the rib–cartilage junctions); **Harrison's sulcus**; **pigeon chest**; widened wrists and ankles; **bow legs** or knock knees; delayed teething and walking; muscle weakness, pot belly; tetany in some.

**Osteomalacia (adults)**: bone pain and tenderness, muscle weakness, waddling gait, fractures; common in women with repeated pregnancies and long lactation who stay indoors.

**Management**: vitamin D and calcium as prescribed; sunlight exposure; calcium-rich diet; orthopaedic care for deformities.

**Prevention**: sunlight on arms and face daily; milk, egg, fish; fortified foods; supplements to at-risk groups as advised.

## 5.7 Iron deficiency anaemia

**Anaemia**: haemoglobin below the normal level for age, sex and physiological state (WHO cut-offs: children 6–59 months below 11 g/dL; non-pregnant women below 12 g/dL; pregnant women below 11 g/dL; men below 13 g/dL). It is the **most common nutritional deficiency in India** — NFHS-5 found about two-thirds of young children and more than half of women of reproductive age anaemic.

**Causes**: low intake of iron (mainly non-haem iron of poor absorption); inhibitors (tea, coffee, phytates); increased need (growth, adolescence, pregnancy); **blood loss** — heavy periods, **hookworm**, bleeding piles, frequent pregnancies, peptic ulcer; malaria; poor absorption.

**Signs and symptoms**: pallor (conjunctiva, tongue, palms, nails); tiredness and weakness; breathlessness and palpitations on exertion; headache, dizziness; poor concentration and school performance; reduced work output; **koilonychia** (spoon nails); angular stomatitis; pica (eating mud, chalk, ice); oedema and heart failure in severe anaemia.

**Diagnosis**: haemoglobin (digital haemoglobinometer used in Anemia Mukt Bharat "Test, Treat, Talk"), peripheral smear (microcytic hypochromic cells), serum ferritin.

**Management**: iron and folic acid treatment as per the national protocol (oral; injectable iron or blood transfusion for severe cases under medical order); treat the cause — deworming, malaria treatment, control of bleeding; iron-rich diet with vitamin C; avoid tea and coffee with meals.

**Prevention**: Anemia Mukt Bharat (prophylactic IFA to six beneficiary groups, deworming, behaviour change communication, testing and treatment, fortified foods — Unit 8); iron-rich diet; cooking in iron vessels; birth spacing; sanitation and footwear (hookworm).

## 5.8 Iodine deficiency disorders (IDD)

**Causes**: low iodine in soil and water (hilly, Himalayan and flood-prone areas, now known to be present all over India); not using iodised salt; goitrogens in large amounts.

**Spectrum of IDD (by life stage)**:

| Stage | Effects |
| --- | --- |
| Foetus | Abortions, stillbirths, congenital anomalies, **cretinism** (dwarfism, intellectual disability, deaf-mutism, squint), higher perinatal deaths |
| Newborn | Neonatal hypothyroidism, goitre |
| Child and adolescent | Goitre, poor school performance, retarded mental and physical growth |
| Adult | **Goitre** and its complications, hypothyroidism (lethargy, weight gain, cold intolerance), reduced work capacity |

**Management**: thyroid hormone or iodine as prescribed; surgery for large goitres causing pressure.

**Prevention**: **universal use of iodised salt** (National Iodine Deficiency Disorders Control Programme, Unit 8); store iodised salt in a closed container away from heat and moisture; add salt after cooking where possible; screening newborns for hypothyroidism where available.

## 5.9 Calcium deficiency

**Causes**: low intake of milk and other calcium foods; vitamin D deficiency; high phytate and oxalate intake; repeated pregnancies and lactation; menopause (falling oestrogen); old age; low parathyroid hormone; kidney disease; long steroid use.

**Signs and symptoms**: in children — rickets, poor growth, delayed teething; in adults — osteomalacia; **osteoporosis** in the elderly and post-menopausal women (back pain, loss of height, stooped back, fractures of hip, wrist and spine after minor falls); **tetany** with low blood calcium — tingling around the mouth and fingers, muscle cramps, carpopedal spasm, convulsions.

**Management**: calcium and vitamin D as prescribed; calcium-rich diet; weight-bearing exercise; fall prevention in the elderly.

**Prevention**: milk, curd, paneer, ragi, sesame, green leafy vegetables; sunlight; regular exercise; avoid smoking and excess alcohol; adequate calcium in adolescence to build peak bone mass.

## 5.10 Nurse's role in deficiency disorders — summary

1. **Identify** at-risk groups (under-fives, adolescent girls, pregnant and lactating women, elderly, poor families).
2. **Assess** — anthropometry, clinical signs, Hb, diet history (Unit 8).
3. **Treat and refer** as per protocol; give supplements and record them.
4. **Educate** on low-cost foods, cooking methods that save nutrients, hygiene and sanitation.
5. **Implement programmes** — ICDS, AMB, vitamin A supplementation, NIDDCP, deworming.
6. **Follow up** and evaluate (weight gain, Hb rise).

## Remember

- WHO: wasting = WFH < −2 SD (acute); stunting = HFA < −2 SD (chronic); underweight = WFA < −2 SD.
- SAM (6–59 months): WFH < −3 SD, MUAC < 11.5 cm, or bilateral pitting oedema. MAM: MUAC 11.5–12.5 cm.
- Kwashiorkor = oedema, flaky paint skin, fatty liver, apathy; marasmus = severe wasting, no oedema, alert, hungry.
- Ten steps for SAM: hypoglycaemia, hypothermia, dehydration, electrolytes, infection, micronutrients (iron later), cautious feeding (F-75), catch-up growth (F-100/RUTF), stimulation, follow-up.
- Night blindness = earliest VAD sign; Bitot's spots = X1B; keratomalacia = blindness.
- Beriberi (B1), angular stomatitis (B2), pellagra 4 D's (niacin), megaloblastic anaemia (folate, B12), scurvy (C), rickets/osteomalacia (D).
- Anaemia cut-offs: pregnant women and young children below 11 g/dL; non-pregnant women below 12; men below 13.
- IDD: goitre, cretinism; prevention by iodised salt.
- Childhood obesity: BMI-for-age above +2 SD (5–19 years).
